subtopic_detail: Investigating young onset hepatitis with a movement disorder and a low alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 22-year-old university student referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver tests found during an insurance medical.

Over the past 6 months his handwriting has become larger and untidy and his housemates have noticed his hands shake when he holds a cup. He has also become withdrawn and has failed a semester after previously passing comfortably. He denies alcohol beyond two drinks a month and takes no paracetamol, supplements or recreational drugs.

His alanine aminotransferase is 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20) and international normalised ratio 1.1. Hepatitis B and C serology are negative, autoimmune liver serology is negative, ferritin and transferrin saturation are within normal limits, and alpha-1 antitrypsin is normal.

His haemoglobin is 108 g/L (130-180) with a direct antiglobulin test that is negative. On examination he has a coarse postural tremor of both arms and mildly slurred speech, with no rigidity and normal power.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor of both arms, mildly slurred speech, no rigidity, normal power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.1, haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), direct antiglobulin test negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, autoimmune liver serology negative, iron studies and alpha-1 antitrypsin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Liver biopsy with histological staging and quantitative tissue iron measurement
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility weighted sequences performed first
Repeat autoimmune liver serology with immunoglobulin subclasses and coeliac antibodies
Serum copper level alone, with a repeat measurement in 4 weeks for confirmation
Serum caeruloplasmin with a 24 hour urinary copper collection and slit lamp examination

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation in a smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 62-year-old man referred with 4 months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home.

He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He also mentions a persistently dry mouth that has made him carry a water bottle everywhere, and erectile difficulty that began around the same time. He has lost 3 kg without trying.

He has no double vision, no drooping eyelids, no difficulty swallowing and no change to his speech, and his symptoms do not fluctuate through the day.

On examination hip flexion and shoulder abduction are both reduced. When he grips your hand and sustains the effort for 15 seconds, his grip strength improves. His knee reflexes are absent on first testing but become obtainable after he contracts the quadriceps for 15 seconds. Sensation is normal. His creatine kinase is within normal limits and his thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction, grip improves after 15 seconds of sustained effort, knee reflexes absent initially but obtainable after sustained quadriceps contraction, normal sensation, no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request acetylcholine receptor antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the mediastinum
Request voltage gated calcium channel antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the chest
Request nerve conduction studies with low frequency repetitive stimulation of a distal nerve
Arrange a muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy
Start prednisolone 50 mg daily and review his proximal strength in the clinic in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Confirmatory testing before commencing targeted therapy for suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 46-year-old woman is referred with 14 months of progressive exertional breathlessness, now limiting her to walking 200 m on the flat, and two episodes of light-headedness on climbing stairs.

She has limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 9 years ago with Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly. She has never smoked and takes nifedipine and a proton pump inhibitor.

On examination there is a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, a left parasternal heave and a jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle. The chest is clear. Spirometry is normal with a diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography shows no interstitial disease and no evidence of emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scanning shows no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure at 62 mmHg with a dilated right ventricle and normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide is 410 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, left parasternal heave, jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle, chest clear, sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry normal with diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: no interstitial disease or emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scan: no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography: estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 62 mmHg, dilated right ventricle, normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide 410 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing before any targeted therapy is commenced
Commence an endothelin receptor antagonist and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
Commence high dose calcium channel blocker therapy and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant and arrange repeat imaging in 3 months
Commence long term oxygen therapy and arrange repeat arterial blood gas measurement in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Management of a congenital repolarisation disorder found during investigation of exertional syncope
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 19-year-old woman is referred after collapsing twice, once while swimming at a carnival and once when a fire alarm sounded unexpectedly at work.

On each occasion she lost consciousness without warning and recovered fully within a minute with no confusion afterward and no tongue biting or incontinence. Her mother describes brief jerking of the limbs during the second episode, lasting a few seconds while she was on the ground.

She takes no medicines and a urine drug screen is negative. A maternal aunt drowned at 22 while swimming in calm water. On examination the cardiovascular examination is normal with no murmur. Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium are within normal limits, as are thyroid function and full blood count. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with normal biventricular function. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 496 ms and broad-based T waves in the precordial leads. An electroencephalogram is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination normal, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 62/min, corrected QT interval 496 ms, broad-based precordial T waves. Echocardiography structurally normal with normal biventricular function. Potassium, magnesium, calcium, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits. Electroencephalogram normal. Urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antiseizure medicine, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
Commence a non-selective beta blocker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
Arrange a permanent pacemaker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
Arrange catheter ablation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for cardiac screening
Commence oral magnesium supplementation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening

subtopic_detail: Acute management when a febrile illness unmasks a type 1 coved ST elevation pattern
stem:
You are the registrar in an emergency department. A 32-year-old man of Vietnamese background presents with 2 days of fever and productive cough. He mentions that he briefly blacked out this morning while getting out of bed and hit his shoulder.

He has had two previous unexplained blackouts at night over 3 years, each attributed to a vasovagal cause. His older brother died suddenly in his sleep at 35 with a normal autopsy.

He takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest has coarse crackles at the right base and the cardiovascular examination is normal. Temperature is 39.1 °C. Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 104 beats per minute with coved ST elevation of 3 mm followed by an inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2, and a corrected QT interval of 400 ms. Potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium are within normal limits, and troponin is not elevated. An electrocardiogram from 2 years ago, taken when he was afebrile, showed only 1 mm of saddleback ST elevation in V1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles at the right base, cardiovascular examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 104/min, coved ST elevation 3 mm with inverted T waves in V1 and V2, corrected QT interval 400 ms. Prior afebrile electrocardiogram 2 years ago: 1 mm saddleback ST elevation in V1 only. Chest radiograph right lower lobe consolidation. Potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, troponin not elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate the catheter laboratory for primary percutaneous coronary intervention for anterior infarction
Commence an intravenous amiodarone infusion and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
Treat the fever aggressively with antipyretics and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
Administer a flecainide challenge to confirm the diagnosis and admit to a monitored bed for observation
Arrange urgent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral

subtopic_detail: Timing intervention for rheumatic mitral stenosis presenting with pulmonary oedema in mid-pregnancy
stem:
You are the registrar in a coronary care unit. A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy is admitted with 4 days of worsening breathlessness, now orthopnoeic and unable to lie flat.

She arrived in Australia from the Pacific at 14 and recalls being told as a child that she had a heart murmur after a febrile illness with sore joints. She has had no cardiology follow-up.

She has responded partially to intravenous furosemide and oxygen in the emergency department. On examination the pulse is 112 beats per minute and irregularly irregular. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. There are crackles to the mid zones bilaterally. Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at 112 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography reports a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2 with a mean gradient of 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus and estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Fetal cardiotocography is normal and growth is on the 45th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 112/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 93% on 4 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud first heart sound, opening snap, low-pitched mid-diastolic apical murmur, bilateral crackles to the mid zones
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: atrial fibrillation at 112/min. Echocardiography: mitral valve area 0.9 cm2, mean gradient 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Cardiotocography normal, growth 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Open mitral valve replacement on cardiopulmonary bypass after rate control and anticoagulation
Continued diuresis with beta blockade alone and planned reassessment in the third trimester
Emergency caesarean birth at 26 weeks followed by valve intervention in the postpartum period
Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty after rate control and anticoagulation are established
Direct current cardioversion to sinus rhythm alone with anticoagulation and no valve intervention

subtopic_detail: Deciding between infective and immune causes of diarrhoea on checkpoint inhibitor therapy
stem:
You are the registrar in an oncology day unit. A 61-year-old man receiving combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for metastatic melanoma presents 5 weeks after his second cycle with 8 days of increasing diarrhoea, now 9 loose stools daily with abdominal cramping and visible blood on two occasions.

He has been opening his bowels twice overnight. He has had no recent travel, no antibiotic exposure and no unwell contacts, and no fever at home.

On examination the abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness and no guarding and no rebound. Bowel sounds are present. Stool testing is negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin, negative on bacterial culture and negative on viral and parasite polymerase chain reaction panel. Cytomegalovirus serology shows past exposure. C-reactive protein is 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180) and faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding and no perforation and no abscess.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, no guarding, no rebound, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Stool Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, bacterial culture negative, viral and parasite panel negative. C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180), faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography: diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding, no perforation or abscess
data_table.Treatment: Combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, second cycle 5 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue immunotherapy and commence loperamide with dietary modification and outpatient review
Withhold immunotherapy and commence oral vancomycin with repeat stool toxin testing in 48 hours
Withhold immunotherapy and commence infliximab as initial therapy with gastroenterology referral
Withhold immunotherapy and arrange urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before commencing any treatment
Withhold immunotherapy and commence high dose systemic corticosteroid with gastroenterology referral

subtopic_detail: Investigation sequencing for progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 41-year-old woman describes 14 months of food sticking behind the sternum, now occurring with both solid food and drinks including water.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has started sleeping propped up. She has lost 5 kg over the past year. She has taken a proton pump inhibitor at full dose for 6 months with no benefit, and says antacids have never helped.

She has no odynophagia, no haematemesis and no hoarseness. She has never smoked and drinks minimal alcohol. On examination she is thin with a body mass index of 19.2 kg/m2, the chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy. Gastroscopy performed last week was reported as showing a normal oesophageal mucosa with no stricture and no mass, with mild resistance passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yielded with gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Anthropometry: Body mass index 19.2 kg/m2, 5 kg weight loss over 12 months
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy: normal oesophageal mucosa, no stricture or mass, mild resistance at the gastro-oesophageal junction yielding to gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with dilatation of the gastro-oesophageal junction under direct vision
Ambulatory 24 hour oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppression therapy
Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast to stage a suspected malignancy
High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and sphincter relaxation
Videofluoroscopic swallow study with a speech pathologist to assess the oropharyngeal phase

subtopic_detail: Next therapeutic step after a proton pump inhibitor trial fails in oesophageal eosinophilia
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 27-year-old man attends for review after an episode 3 months ago in which a piece of steak lodged in his oesophagus and required endoscopic removal.

He has a long history of asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. He describes years of food sticking that he had adapted to by chewing extensively, cutting food finely and drinking water with every mouthful.

At the index endoscopy the oesophagus showed concentric rings and longitudinal furrows with white exudate, and biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus each showed 45 eosinophils per high power field. He was commenced on a proton pump inhibitor at full dose twice daily. A repeat endoscopy last week, after 10 weeks of therapy, shows persisting rings and furrows and biopsies showing 38 eosinophils per high power field. He reports no improvement in his swallowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Index endoscopy: concentric rings, longitudinal furrows, white exudate; proximal and distal biopsies 45 eosinophils per high power field. Repeat endoscopy after 10 weeks of twice daily proton pump inhibitor: persisting rings and furrows, biopsies 38 eosinophils per high power field
data_table.History: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, childhood eczema; food impaction requiring endoscopic removal 3 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a long-acting inhaled corticosteroid by metered dose inhaler and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
Commence oral prednisolone at a weaning dose and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
Arrange skin prick testing to guide a targeted food elimination diet and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
Arrange endoscopic oesophageal dilatation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
Commence a swallowed topical corticosteroid preparation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Deciding which patient with airflow obstruction warrants testing for an inherited protease inhibitor deficiency
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 43-year-old woman is referred with 2 years of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily cough productive of clear sputum.

She has never smoked and has worked as a primary school teacher. She has no history of childhood asthma and no occupational dust or fume exposure. Her brother was diagnosed with emphysema at 47 and her father died of liver cirrhosis at 58 with no history of alcohol use.

She takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest is hyperinflated with quiet breath sounds throughout and no wheeze. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, with a 4 per cent improvement after bronchodilator. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography of the chest reports panlobular emphysema most marked in the lower zones. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function tests are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Hyperinflated chest with quiet breath sounds throughout, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, 4 per cent post-bronchodilator improvement. Chest radiograph hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography: panlobular lower zone emphysema. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration, with phenotyping if the level is reduced
Serum total immunoglobulin E with specific aeroallergen testing, and skin prick testing if elevated
Sweat chloride testing, with cystic fibrosis gene panel analysis if the result is elevated
Serum angiotensin converting enzyme, with tissue biopsy if the level is elevated
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing, with renal biopsy if the titre is elevated

subtopic_detail: Confirming a workplace cause for adult onset asthma before recommending removal from exposure
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 34-year-old man is referred with 8 months of cough, chest tightness and wheeze that began 2 years after he started work as a spray painter in a vehicle repair shop.

He reports symptoms build through the working week and are noticeably better on weekends and were absent during a 3 week holiday. He uses a supplied respirator inconsistently. He has never smoked and had no childhood asthma or atopy.

On examination the chest is clear today, having been reviewed on a Monday morning. Spirometry today shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted) with a ratio of 0.79 and a 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph is normal. Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5). He is worried about losing his job and asks whether he really has to leave the trade.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, assessed on a Monday morning
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted), ratio 0.79, 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph normal. Eosinophil count 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)
data_table.Occupational: Spray painter for approximately 3 years; symptoms build across the working week, resolve at weekends and during a 3 week holiday; inconsistent respirator use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise immediate permanent removal from spray painting work and commence inhaled corticosteroid therapy
Arrange serial peak expiratory flow recordings across periods at work and away from work
Commence inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist and continue current work practices
Arrange high resolution computed tomography of the chest to assess for an interstitial process
Arrange skin prick testing to common aeroallergens to establish an atopic basis for the symptoms

subtopic_detail: Bedside manoeuvres separating dynamic outflow obstruction from fixed valvular stenosis
stem:
You are the resident in a cardiology clinic. A 24-year-old man is referred after collapsing while playing football. He describes a few seconds of greying vision as he sprinted, then waking on the ground with bystanders around him.

He has had two similar near-collapses while exercising over the past year, each resolving within a minute of stopping. He has no chest pain at rest and no palpitations. His father died suddenly at 41 while swimming and no autopsy findings were ever discussed with the family.

On examination the pulse is sharp with a rapid upstroke. The apex beat is forceful and undisplaced with a palpable double impulse. There is a harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that does not radiate to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder when he stands from squatting and softer during a sustained handgrip. There is no ejection click. Electrocardiogram shows deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Sharp pulse with rapid upstroke, forceful undisplaced apex with palpable double impulse, harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge without carotid radiation, louder on standing from squatting, softer with sustained handgrip, no ejection click
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: deep narrow Q waves inferolaterally with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Fixed valvular aortic stenosis from a calcified congenitally bicuspid valve
Ventricular septal defect with left to right shunting across a perimembranous defect
Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction from asymmetric septal hypertrophy
Mitral valve prolapse with late systolic regurgitation through a myxomatous valve
Pulmonary valve stenosis with right ventricular overload and post-stenotic dilatation

subtopic_detail: Obligations and screening after silicosis is identified in an engineered stone benchtop worker
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 38-year-old man is referred with 10 months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has cut and polished engineered stone benchtops in a fabrication workshop for 9 years, frequently dry cutting without water suppression.

He has never smoked. He reports no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats, and no joint pain, rash or dry eyes.

On examination there is no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy and fine inspiratory crackles at both bases. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, with a diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography reports multiple small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with an upper zone predominance, with enlarged hilar nodes showing peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis is negative, and antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: No clubbing or lymphadenopathy, fine inspiratory crackles at both bases
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with upper zone predominance, hilar nodes with peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay negative, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at an immunosuppressive dose and continue current work with a fitted respirator
Commence antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib and continue current work with a fitted respirator
Commence a standard four drug antituberculous regimen and continue current work with a fitted respirator
Notify the occupational health authority, remove him from further exposure and screen co-workers
Arrange surgical lung biopsy to confirm the histological pattern before making any workplace recommendation

subtopic_detail: Separating pericardial constriction from myocardial restriction after mediastinal radiotherapy
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 54-year-old woman presents with 8 months of progressive abdominal swelling and ankle oedema. She was treated for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 26 with mediastinal radiotherapy and remains in remission.

She describes breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs but sleeps flat on one pillow. She has had two paracenteses at another hospital, each time being told the fluid was a transudate, and was investigated for liver disease with a normal liver biopsy.

On examination the jugular venous pressure is elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rises on inspiration. There is tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees and a firm non-pulsatile liver edge. Heart sounds are normal with an added early diastolic sound. Echocardiography reports normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valve appearances, a respirophasic ventricular septal shift and marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide is 128 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rising on inspiration, tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees, firm non-pulsatile liver edge, added early diastolic sound
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography: normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valves, respirophasic ventricular septal shift, marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide 128 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from infiltration producing impaired myocardial relaxation and compliance
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension producing ascites and secondary peripheral fluid retention
Severe tricuspid regurgitation producing systolic venous congestion and secondary hepatic enlargement
Pulmonary arterial hypertension producing right ventricular pressure overload and systemic congestion
Pericardial constriction producing equalisation of diastolic pressures between the cardiac chambers

subtopic_detail: Timing of ventilatory support in motor neuron disease using supine vital capacity and nocturnal symptoms
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a neurology clinic reviewing a 61-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis fourteen months ago. He has been taking riluzole since diagnosis and attends a multidisciplinary clinic every three months.

He tells you he now sleeps 'propped up on four pillows' because lying flat makes him feel he cannot get enough air, wakes two or three times a night, and has a dull headache for the first hour after waking that clears by mid-morning. He dozes off in the afternoon, which is new.

He has wasting of both hands with fasciculations, brisk reflexes and mild dysarthria, but swallows normally and his weight is stable. Forced vital capacity is 68 per cent predicted sitting and falls to 52 per cent predicted when supine. Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension is 44 mmHg. Overnight oximetry shows the oxygen saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96 per cent on room air seated, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Respiratory symptoms: Orthopnoea requiring four pillows, two to three nocturnal awakenings, morning headache clearing by mid-morning, new daytime somnolence
data_table.Lung function: Forced vital capacity 68 per cent predicted sitting, falling to 52 per cent predicted supine
data_table.Gas exchange: Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension 44 mmHg; overnight oximetry with saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording
data_table.Neurological and nutritional: Wasted fasciculating hands, brisk reflexes, mild dysarthria, normal swallow, stable weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start riluzole and review his respiratory function again in three months
Arrange a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy before any other intervention
Start nocturnal oxygen by nasal prongs at 2 L/min and review him in one month
Refer now for assessment and initiation of non-invasive nocturnal ventilation
Start morphine and a benzodiazepine for breathlessness and review in a month

subtopic_detail: Choosing the initial screening test when acral and facial change suggests growth hormone excess
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44-year-old man referred with bilateral hand numbness that wakes him at night and is worst in the thumb and index finger. He mentions in passing that he has had his wedding ring enlarged twice and has gone up two shoe sizes in five years.

His wife, who attends with him, says his jaw 'looks heavier' and produces a photograph from eight years ago that shows noticeably finer features and a smaller nose.

On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, there is an interdental gap that he says is new, and the tongue appears enlarged. Tinel sign is positive bilaterally at the wrist. Blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg on two occasions and fasting glucose is 6.6 mmol/L. He has no headache and no visual symptoms, and confrontation visual fields are full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two occasions, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Broad hands with doughy soft tissue, new interdental separation, enlarged tongue, coarsened facial features against a photograph from eight years ago
data_table.Neurological: Tinel sign positive bilaterally at the wrist; confrontation visual fields full
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level as the initial screening test
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary as the initial investigation
Measure a serum insulin-like growth factor 1 as the initial screening test
Measure an early morning serum cortisol as the initial screening investigation
Arrange a 48 hour low dose dexamethasone suppression test as the first step

subtopic_detail: Dorsal column signs with a serum cobalamin inside the reference range in a recreational inhalant user
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 24-year-old hospitality worker referred with six weeks of numbness and tingling that began in both feet and has ascended to just below both knees. He says he now has to 'watch my feet to know where they are' and stumbles badly in a dark corridor.

He eats a mixed diet including meat and dairy, has had no gastrointestinal surgery and takes no metformin or proton pump inhibitor. When asked directly about recreational drugs he tells you he inhales nitrous oxide from cream chargers, roughly a hundred bulbs a week for the past eight months.

On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent while both plantar responses are extensor. Power is preserved. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Neurological examination: Vibration absent at ankles and reduced at knees, impaired joint position sense at the great toes, Romberg positive, ankle reflexes absent with extensor plantar responses, power preserved
data_table.Investigations: Serum vitamin B12 210 pmol/L (150-700), haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 92 fL (80-98), no hypersegmented neutrophils on film
data_table.Metabolites: Serum homocysteine 42 micromol/L (5-15), methylmalonic acid 1.9 micromol/L (less than 0.4)
data_table.Exposure: Nitrous oxide inhalation, approximately 100 bulbs weekly for eight months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that the vitamin B12 level is normal and repeat it in three months
Start oral cyanocobalamin 1000 microgram daily and review him in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine before starting any treatment
Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review his neurological signs in one month
Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now and advise him to stop the nitrous oxide

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice for venous thrombosis in a patient with an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67-year-old man on the oncology ward. He was diagnosed six weeks ago with a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and started neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and today his left calf and thigh have become swollen and painful.

His endoscopy report describes a large ulcerated antral lesion, and he has needed two units of red cells since diagnosis for a slow drop in haemoglobin attributed to tumour ooze. He has had no melaena or haematemesis this admission.

Doppler ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. His platelet count is 120 x10^9/L, creatinine clearance is 78 mL/min and liver function is within normal limits. He is taking no antiplatelet drugs and has a central venous access device in the right arm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Imaging: Doppler ultrasound shows occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins
data_table.Tumour: Large ulcerated gastric antral adenocarcinoma, unresected, on neoadjuvant chemotherapy
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 120 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine clearance 78 mL/min, liver function within normal limits, haemoglobin 98 g/L (130-180) after two units of red cells
data_table.Other: No antiplatelet drugs; central venous access device in the right arm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Start oral apixaban at a treatment dose and continue while the cancer is active
Start subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin at a treatment dose and continue
Start warfarin with heparin bridging and target a ratio of 2 to 3 thereafter
Insert a retrievable inferior vena cava filter and withhold anticoagulation
Start oral rivaroxaban at a treatment dose and continue for three months only

subtopic_detail: High anion gap acidosis with a raised osmolar gap and urinary crystals in a patient with no visual symptoms
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 47-year-old man found drowsy on his garage floor by his brother, who says he drinks heavily and has been low since losing his job. He last ate yesterday morning.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused and is breathing deeply and rapidly. He has vomited twice since arrival. He tells you his vision is completely normal and reads the wall clock across the room without difficulty, and his pupils are 4 mm and briskly reactive with normal fundi.

His brother brings in a partly empty 2 litre container of engine coolant from beside him and also a bottle of methylated spirits, and does not know whether either was opened today. Point-of-care glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. Investigations are shown. Urine microscopy reports abundant envelope shaped crystals and the urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min and deep, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1°C
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.06, arterial carbon dioxide tension 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 102 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 198 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 5.4 mmol/L, serum ketones 0.2 mmol/L (less than 0.6)
data_table.Osmolality: Measured serum osmolality 340 mOsm/kg (275-295); calculated osmolarity 302 mOsm/L
data_table.Urine and vision: Abundant envelope shaped crystals on microscopy, urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp; visual acuity normal, pupils 4 mm and briskly reactive, fundi normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give fomepizole now and arrange urgent haemodialysis with the renal team
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate alone and repeat the blood gas in an hour
Give intravenous thiamine and dextrose and repeat the blood gas in an hour
Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
Give intravenous N-acetylcysteine and arrange urgent liver function testing

subtopic_detail: Timeframe for colonoscopy after a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test in the national program
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 62-year-old man who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from his National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit. He completed it three weeks ago and says he 'nearly threw the envelope out because I feel completely fine'.

He has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit and no abdominal pain. His weight has been stable for years. There is no family history of bowel cancer or polyps and he has never had a colonoscopy.

He takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Examination including abdominal and rectal examination is unremarkable. A full blood count taken last month for another reason showed a haemoglobin of 148 g/L (130-180) with a mean cell volume of 89 fL (80-98).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Screening result: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program
data_table.Symptoms: No rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no abdominal pain, weight stable
data_table.Examination: Abdominal and rectal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-98)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in twelve months' time
Arrange a computed tomography colonography within the next thirty days
Refer for colonoscopy to be performed within thirty days of the result
Check a full blood count and iron studies and refer only if he is anaemic
Refer for flexible sigmoidoscopy to be performed within thirty days

subtopic_detail: Choosing a repeat intravenous iron preparation after symptomatic hypophosphataemia from the previous infusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a haematology clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding. She has a levonorgestrel intrauterine system in place and is awaiting gynaecological review.

Oral ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation at every dose she tried, including alternate day dosing, and she stopped it after two months. She was given an intravenous infusion of ferric carboxymaltose three months ago.

Two weeks after that infusion she developed profound fatigue, aching in both thighs and pain in her ribs when she coughed, and a serum phosphate taken at the time was 0.42 mmol/L. The symptoms and the phosphate normalised over eight weeks without specific treatment. Her haemoglobin has now fallen again and she needs further parenteral iron.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Current investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-98), ferritin 8 microgram/L (15-200), transferrin saturation 6 per cent (15-45)
data_table.Previous episode: Serum phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) two weeks after ferric carboxymaltose, with fatigue, thigh ache and rib pain; normalised over eight weeks
data_table.Oral iron history: Ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation including on alternate day dosing; stopped after two months
data_table.Renal and bone profile: Creatinine, corrected calcium and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ferric carboxymaltose and check the serum phosphate two weeks later
Give ferric derisomaltose instead and check the serum phosphate afterwards
Restart oral ferrous sulfate daily and check the haemoglobin in three months
Give oral phosphate supplements and repeat the ferric carboxymaltose today
Transfuse two units of red cells and check the serum ferritin afterwards

subtopic_detail: Initiating iron removal in a C282Y homozygote with a markedly raised ferritin and no fibrosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a liver clinic seeing a 48-year-old man referred after abnormal blood tests taken for life insurance. He says he feels 'a bit flat and achy in the knuckles' but has no other complaints.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no regular medications, vitamins or iron supplements. His father died at 61 of liver disease that was never fully investigated.

His fasting transferrin saturation is 62 per cent with a ferritin of 1150 microgram/L, repeated on a second fasting sample with the same values. HFE genotyping reports homozygosity for the C282Y variant. Alanine aminotransferase is mildly raised, C-reactive protein is within normal limits and transient elastography reports a liver stiffness of 4.8 kPa. Fasting glucose and an echocardiogram are both normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Iron studies: Fasting transferrin saturation 62 per cent (15-45), ferritin 1150 microgram/L (30-300), confirmed on a repeat fasting sample
data_table.Genetics: HFE genotype homozygous for the C282Y variant
data_table.Liver assessment: Alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 45), C-reactive protein within normal limits, transient elastography 4.8 kPa
data_table.Other results: Fasting glucose and echocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral deferasirox and repeat the ferritin measurement in three months
Start weekly venesection aiming for a ferritin of 50 to 100 microgram/L
Advise dietary iron restriction and repeat the ferritin in twelve months
Arrange liver biopsy before any decision about starting iron removal
Repeat the iron studies fasting in three months before starting treatment

subtopic_detail: Action on a first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in stable bronchiectasis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a respiratory clinic seeing a 56-year-old woman with bronchiectasis confirmed on high resolution computed tomography five years ago following childhood pertussis. She attends for a routine review and says she is 'about the same as always'.

She produces around 20 mL of mucoid sputum daily, has had no increase in volume or change in colour, no fever and no new breathlessness, and has not had an exacerbation for eight months. She performs airway clearance twice daily and her forced expiratory volume in one second is unchanged from six months ago at 72 per cent predicted.

Her previous sputum cultures over five years have consistently grown Haemophilus influenzae. The routine sputum sample collected at her last visit has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa for the first time, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and to tobramycin.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Symptoms: 20 mL mucoid sputum daily, unchanged; no fever, no new breathlessness, no exacerbation for eight months
data_table.Lung function: Forced expiratory volume in one second 72 per cent predicted, unchanged from six months ago
data_table.Microbiology: First isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and tobramycin; all previous cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attempt eradication with oral ciprofloxacin and nebulised tobramycin
Start long term azithromycin three times weekly and repeat the sputum culture
Observe and repeat the sputum culture in three months if she remains well
Start inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist and review her
Refer for surgical resection of the most affected bronchiectatic segment

subtopic_detail: Withdrawing a long standing nightly benzodiazepine after recurrent falls in an older woman
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing an 82-year-old woman in a falls clinic. She has fallen twice in three months, once in the hallway on the way to the toilet at 2 am and once getting out of bed in the morning, and says she 'just went down' both times with no warning and no chest pain or palpitations.

She lives alone in a single storey unit and manages her own shopping. She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eleven years, originally started after her husband died, and says she 'could not possibly sleep without it'. She also takes sertraline 50 mg daily and perindopril.

Lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop. Gait is slow but steady with a normal timed up and go test, visual acuity is corrected to 6/9 bilaterally and cognition is intact. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate is 48 mL/min/1.73m2. An electrocardiogram and a vitamin D level are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Medications: Temazepam 20 mg nightly for eleven years, sertraline 50 mg daily, perindopril
data_table.Falls assessment: Timed up and go test within normal limits, gait slow but steady, corrected visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2, electrocardiogram and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the temazepam tonight and start modified release melatonin instead
Continue the temazepam and refer her to a falls prevention program only
Reduce the temazepam by about a quarter every two to four weeks with support
Switch her to nightly zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review in a month
Switch her to nightly diazepam at an equivalent dose and review in a month

subtopic_detail: Advising a man in his mid fifties whose father was diagnosed with prostate cancer after age sixty
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 55-year-old man for a routine review of his blood pressure. Towards the end of the consultation he says a colleague has told him to 'get the prostate test' and asks whether he should have it.

His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 62 and is alive and well eight years after treatment. He has no brothers. No other family members have had prostate, breast or ovarian cancer.

He passes urine twice a night, which he says has been the same for years, with a normal stream and no haematuria and no bone pain. Digital rectal examination has never been performed. He is otherwise well, works full time, and tells you he would want treatment if something were found.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Family history: Father diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 62 and well eight years after treatment; no brothers; no family history of breast or ovarian cancer
data_table.Urinary symptoms: Nocturia twice nightly, unchanged for years, normal stream, no haematuria
data_table.Other: No bone pain, works full time, would accept treatment if a cancer were found

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Arrange a prostate specific antigen test and a digital rectal examination today
Advise against testing and review him again when he turns sixty years old
Refer him directly to urology for multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging
Arrange a prostate specific antigen test yearly from now until age seventy
Discuss the benefits and harms and recommend two yearly testing to age 69

subtopic_detail: Rash with fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis six weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 64-year-old man from the emergency department with a rash and fever. He says it started around his neck nine days ago and 'has taken over everywhere', and that his face feels tight and swollen.

He started allopurinol 300 mg daily six weeks ago for recurrent gout. He takes perindopril and has taken no new antibiotics, herbal preparations or over the counter medicines.

On examination there is a confluent morbilliform eruption covering the trunk, both arms and both legs with marked periorbital and facial oedema. The lips, conjunctivae and oral mucosa are unaffected, there is no skin detachment and Nikolsky sign is negative. There is tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9°C
data_table.Skin: Confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk and all four limbs with facial and periorbital oedema; mucosae spared; no skin detachment; Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with atypical lymphocytes, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 88 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Allopurinol 300 mg daily started six weeks ago; perindopril long term

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start topical corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine
Continue the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
Stop the allopurinol and transfer him to a burns unit for specialist skin care
Stop the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
Stop the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin over five days

subtopic_detail: diagnosis and therapy for prolonged fever with hepatitis in an abattoir worker
stem:
You are the general practitioner in a regional town seeing a 38-year-old man with three weeks of fever, drenching sweats, severe retro-orbital headache and profound fatigue. He has lost 5 kg. He works on the kill floor of the local abattoir and helped with a sheep shearing weekend a month ago. He has not travelled overseas.

He has taken two courses of amoxicillin from an after hours service without benefit. Examination shows a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits, a tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no lymphadenopathy, no rash and no murmur. Alanine aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin within normal limits, white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400) and C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5). Chest radiograph and two sets of blood cultures are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; no lymphadenopathy, rash, splinter haemorrhages or murmur
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40); alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110); bilirubin within normal limits; white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400); C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5); chest radiograph normal; two sets of blood cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat blood cultures while febrile and commence intravenous ceftriaxone empirically pending those culture results
Send paired phase I and phase II serology and commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a two week course
Send Brucella serology and commence oral rifampicin with doxycycline for a six week combination course
Send hepatitis A, B and C serology and manage him supportively pending the results of that viral screen
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to investigate a possible occult lymphoproliferative disorder

subtopic_detail: treatment of an acute crystal arthritis with rhomboid crystals in a patient with renal impairment
stem:
You are the doctor on a medical ward. A 78-year-old woman admitted four days ago with community-acquired pneumonia has developed a hot, swollen, exquisitely painful left knee overnight. She has never had joint problems before and does not drink alcohol.

Temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion and she resists all movement. A plain radiograph shows a thin line of calcification within the meniscal cartilage and the hyaline articular cartilage. Joint aspiration yields cloudy yellow fluid with 22 000 white cells per microlitre, predominantly neutrophils, a negative Gram stain, and rhomboid crystals showing weak positive birefringence under polarised light. Her creatinine is 168 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1.73m2, and her serum urate is 0.32 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.45).

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Warm left knee with moderate effusion, marked tenderness and resistance to passive movement; no overlying skin breach or cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Knee radiograph shows linear calcification in meniscal and hyaline cartilage; synovial fluid 22 000 white cells per microlitre predominantly neutrophils, Gram stain negative, rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence; creatinine 168 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 26 mL/min/1.73m2; serum urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.45)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment while cultures are pending?

options.text: Commence a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug at full dose with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
Commence allopurinol at a low dose and titrate upward against a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed septic arthritis and arrange arthroscopic washout of the joint today
Perform an intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the knee once the synovial fluid culture has been reported as negative
Commence oral colchicine at a loading dose followed by twice daily maintenance until the joint symptoms have settled

subtopic_detail: interpreting visible haematuria occurring at the same time as a sore throat rather than weeks later
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old man who noticed his urine turned the colour of dark tea yesterday. He developed a sore throat two days ago and the urine change began on the second day of the throat symptoms. He recalls a similar episode of dark urine two years ago during a chest infection, which cleared within a week and was not investigated.

He has no dysuria, no frequency, no flank pain and no recent exercise or trauma. Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits. There is no oedema, no rash and no joint swelling. Urine microscopy shows numerous dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts. Urine protein to creatinine ratio is 68 mg/mmol. Creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 88 mL/min/1.73m2. Complement C3 and C4 are within normal limits, antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody are negative, and an antistreptolysin O titre is not raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No peripheral or periorbital oedema; no rash or purpura; no synovitis; pharynx mildly injected
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts; urine protein to creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol; creatinine 96 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody negative; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor targeting a blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg and refer to nephrology
Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin for the pharyngitis and repeat the urinalysis in four weeks once the infection has resolved
Arrange a computed tomography urogram and cystoscopy to exclude a urothelial or renal tract source for the visible haematuria
Commence oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg daily and arrange nephrology review once the corticosteroid course is completed
Reassure him that this represents a benign familial thin basement membrane condition and arrange annual urinalysis review

subtopic_detail: workup of an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with localised bone pain and deformity
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old man who has had a deep ache in his right shin for eight months, worse at night and present at rest. He mentions that his hats have become tighter over the last two years and that he has noticed some hearing loss on the right.

He is otherwise well and takes no medication. On examination the right tibia is bowed anteriorly and feels warm compared with the left. Alkaline phosphatase is 684 U/L (30 to 110), with gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin all within normal limits. Corrected calcium is 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate is within normal limits, parathyroid hormone is within normal limits, 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L (50 to 150) and creatinine is within normal limits. A radiograph of the tibia shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation and an area of lucency with a flame shaped advancing edge.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anterior bowing of the right tibia with overlying warmth; increased skull circumference reported; reduced hearing on the right
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 684 U/L (30 to 110); gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin within normal limits; corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60); phosphate, parathyroid hormone and creatinine within normal limits; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (50 to 150); tibial radiograph shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation and a flame shaped lucent advancing front

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with oral calcium supplementation and recheck the bone profile after twelve weeks
Commence oral denosumab equivalent antiresorptive therapy every six months and monitor the alkaline phosphatase annually
Arrange a radionuclide bone scan to define the extent of disease and give a single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion
Repeat the alkaline phosphatase with liver function tests in three months and investigate further only if it continues to rise
Arrange a bone biopsy of the tibial lesion to exclude an underlying primary bone malignancy before commencing any treatment

subtopic_detail: treating a painless genital ulcer with a positive treponemal screen and reactive rapid plasma reagin
stem:
You are the doctor in a sexual health clinic seeing a 31-year-old man who noticed a sore on his penis ten days ago. It does not hurt and he only sought review because it has not healed. He has had three male partners in the past six months and uses condoms inconsistently. He takes tenofovir with emtricitabine as pre-exposure prophylaxis and his last human immunodeficiency virus test six weeks ago was negative.

On examination there is a single 1 cm ulcer on the coronal sulcus with a clean indurated base and a rolled edge, and it is not tender to touch. There are firm, non-tender, mobile inguinal nodes bilaterally. There is no rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no oral lesion and no alopecia. Treponemal enzyme immunoassay is reactive, rapid plasma reagin titre is 1 in 32, and a swab of the ulcer base is positive for Treponema pallidum on polymerase chain reaction. Repeat human immunodeficiency virus serology and nucleic acid testing are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Single 1 cm indurated painless ulcer with a clean base at the coronal sulcus; firm non-tender mobile bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy; no truncal, palmar or plantar rash; no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive; rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32; ulcer base polymerase chain reaction positive for Treponema pallidum; human immunodeficiency virus serology and nucleic acid testing negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
A fourteen day course of oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 500 mg with a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g, and contact tracing
A ten day course of oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
A single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months

subtopic_detail: empirical therapy for cavitating pneumonia in a diabetic patient during the northern wet season
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a Northern Territory regional hospital in February. A 54-year-old man is admitted with five days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 9.8 per cent and drinks heavily. He works as a landscaper and has been digging in flooded ground after recent heavy rain.

Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 90 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius. Chest examination reveals right sided bronchial breathing. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe consolidation containing two thin walled cavities, and computed tomography of the abdomen performed for pain shows three small hypodense splenic lesions. White cell count is 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60 to 110), lactate 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0) and blood cultures are flagging as positive with Gram negative bacilli.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 90 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right sided bronchial breathing with dullness to percussion; no skin lesions; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows right upper lobe consolidation with two thin walled cavities; computed tomography abdomen shows three small hypodense splenic lesions; white cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); creatinine 142 micromol/L (60 to 110); lactate 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0); glycated haemoglobin 9.8 per cent; blood cultures positive with Gram negative bacilli

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, treating for an invasive fungal infection given his poorly controlled diabetes
Intravenous meropenem, with a plan for prolonged oral eradication therapy after the intensive intravenous phase
Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline, escalating if there is no clinical response over the next 48 hours
Intravenous flucloxacillin with intravenous gentamicin, covering staphylococcal cavitating pneumonia with metastatic seeding
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and a single dose of intravenous gentamicin, reviewing once susceptibilities return

subtopic_detail: preventing circulatory dysfunction when a large volume of ascitic fluid is drained in one sitting
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with alcohol related cirrhosis who has been admitted with abdominal distension. She stopped drinking a year ago. She is breathless lying flat, cannot eat more than a few mouthfuls before feeling full, and has gained 9 kg over six weeks.

She already takes spironolactone 400 mg and furosemide 160 mg daily, the maximum tolerated doses, and has been adherent on a 5 g sodium diet. Her abdomen is tensely distended with obvious shifting dullness and her umbilicus is everted. Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. A diagnostic tap shows 90 neutrophils per microlitre with a serum ascites albumin gradient of 16 g/L. Creatinine is 104 micromol/L (45 to 90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145), albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50) and international normalised ratio 1.4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tensely distended abdomen with shifting dullness and everted umbilicus; orthopnoea; no encephalopathy or asterixis; no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic neutrophil count 90 per microlitre with serum ascites albumin gradient 16 g/L; creatinine 104 micromol/L (45 to 90); sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145); albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50); international normalised ratio 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the diuretic doses further and restrict her dietary sodium more strictly, reviewing her weight and electrolytes daily
Correct her coagulation with fresh frozen plasma before any drainage, given the raised international normalised ratio and low platelets
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone with albumin on days one and three, treating the ascitic fluid as infected pending culture
Perform a large volume paracentesis to dryness and infuse intravenous albumin at about 8 g for every litre of fluid removed
Perform a large volume paracentesis to dryness and replace the fluid with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent as needed

subtopic_detail: screening before immunosuppression in a patient from a region endemic for a persistent helminth
stem:
You are the doctor in a rheumatology clinic planning treatment for a 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis. She is about to start prednisolone 50 mg daily with a plan to add tocilizumab.

She was born in a remote community in the Top End and lived there until she was 30, often walking barefoot. She has lived in Melbourne for 28 years and has not returned. She is well apart from the arteritis, has no gastrointestinal symptoms and no cough. Her full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), with the rest of the count, renal function and liver function within normal limits. Hepatitis B and C serology and an interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis are all negative, and her chest radiograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash, no abdominal tenderness, no respiratory signs; temporal arteries thickened and tender
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophil count 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5) with remainder of full blood count within normal limits; renal and liver function within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serology negative; interferon gamma release assay negative; chest radiograph normal

lead_in: What additional step should be taken before starting immunosuppression?

options.text: Send Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if it is positive, or treat presumptively if the result will be delayed
Send three stool specimens for ova, cysts and parasites and proceed with immunosuppression if all three are negative
Repeat the eosinophil count in four weeks and investigate for a parasitic cause only if the eosinophilia persists or rises
Commence prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the duration of her corticosteroid therapy and proceed as planned
Arrange a bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood flow cytometry to investigate the unexplained eosinophilia before treatment

subtopic_detail: separating volume overload from an immune reaction when dyspnoea follows a red cell transfusion
stem:
You are the doctor on a medical ward called to a 79-year-old woman who has become breathless. She is receiving her second unit of red cells for iron deficiency anaemia from chronic gastrointestinal blood loss, and the unit is 40 minutes in. She has a history of chronic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and takes furosemide, which was withheld this morning.

Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 88 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The jugular venous pressure is elevated at 6 cm above the sternal angle, there are bilateral basal crackles and new pitting oedema to the mid shins. There is no rash, no urticaria, no wheeze and no back or loin pain. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates with upper lobe venous diversion and small pleural effusions, and the cardiothoracic ratio is increased compared with a film from last year.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 88 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated 6 cm above the sternal angle; bilateral basal crackles; new pitting oedema to mid shins; no rash, urticaria or wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates, upper lobe venous diversion, small bilateral pleural effusions and an increased cardiothoracic ratio compared with a prior film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop the transfusion, send the unit and a clotted sample for a haemolysis workup, and commence intravenous fluid to protect renal function
Slow the transfusion rate, give oral paracetamol and an antihistamine, and complete the remainder of the unit under closer observation
Stop the transfusion, sit her upright with oxygen, and give an intravenous loop diuretic with close monitoring of her response
Stop the transfusion, give supportive oxygen and consider ventilatory support, and avoid diuretics as the intravascular volume is not raised
Stop the transfusion, give intramuscular adrenaline and intravenous fluid, and commence a continuous adrenaline infusion if required

subtopic_detail: confirming reversibility before referring a gait and continence syndrome for a shunt
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar assessing a 76-year-old man referred with fourteen months of progressive walking difficulty. His wife says his feet seem stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and when he turns, though he walks better holding a trolley. He has had urinary urgency for six months with three episodes of incontinence. She also reports that he is slower to answer questions and has lost interest in the newspaper.

He has no resting tremor and his arm swing is preserved. His steps are short with a wide base and outwardly rotated feet, and he takes six steps to turn. He scores 24 out of 30 on a cognitive screen with the losses in attention and executive items and preserved recall. A three month trial of levodopa at adequate dose produced no change. Magnetic resonance imaging shows ventriculomegaly with an Evans index of 0.37, a callosal angle of 62 degrees, and tight high convexity sulci with enlarged sylvian fissures. There is mild small vessel change but no infarct.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Magnetic gait with short wide based steps, outward foot rotation and a six step turn; preserved arm swing; no resting tremor; no cogwheel rigidity; cognitive screen 24 out of 30 with attentional and executive losses and preserved recall
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging shows Evans index 0.37, callosal angle 62 degrees, tight high convexity sulci with enlarged sylvian fissures, mild small vessel change and no infarct; no response to a three month trial of levodopa

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion on the basis of the clinical triad and the supporting imaging findings
Increase the levodopa dose substantially and reassess his gait after a further eight weeks of higher dose therapy
Attribute the syndrome to cerebral small vessel disease, optimise vascular risk factors and refer for gait rehabilitation
Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for probable Alzheimer disease and arrange formal neuropsychological assessment in six months
Perform a high volume lumbar puncture with quantified gait timing before and after, and refer to neurosurgery if he improves

subtopic_detail: sequencing cooling and transfer in exertional hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction
stem:
You are the doctor at a medical tent at a summer fun run when a 24-year-old man collapses 400 m from the finish. The ambient temperature is 36 degrees Celsius with high humidity. He is confused, combative and does not know where he is. Bystanders say he was running normally until he staggered and fell.

He is not a known epileptic, takes no regular medication and has taken no recreational drugs according to his running partner. Pulse rate 148 per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, rectal temperature 41.6 degrees Celsius. His skin is hot and sweaty. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. There is no neck stiffness, no rash and no head injury. The tent has ice, several large tubs of water, intravenous fluids and a monitor. The nearest emergency department is fifteen minutes away by road and an ambulance has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, rectal temperature 41.6 degrees Celsius
