data_table.Examination: Confused and combative with no orientation to place; skin hot and sweaty; no neck stiffness, rash or evidence of head injury; capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give intravenous midazolam to control the agitation and reassess his temperature once he is settled and safe to handle
Begin cold water immersion on site immediately and continue until the core temperature falls to about 39 degrees Celsius
Transfer him urgently by ambulance with the air conditioning on maximum and commence active cooling on arrival at hospital
Give intravenous paracetamol and cold intravenous fluid, then apply ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck while awaiting transport
Give intravenous dantrolene and commence aggressive crystalloid resuscitation while arranging urgent transfer to intensive care

subtopic_detail: modifying the resuscitation algorithm when cardiac arrest occurs at a very low core temperature
stem:
You are the doctor receiving a 46-year-old bushwalker retrieved from an alpine area after a night lost in sleet. He was found unresponsive. On arrival he is in cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation on the monitor, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is in progress.

His oesophageal temperature reads 27.4 degrees Celsius. He has been shocked once at the scene without response and has received no drugs. He is intubated with good chest rise and end tidal carbon dioxide of 14 mmHg. His clothing has been cut away and he is being dried. Potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 6.2 mmol/L and lactate 7 mmol/L (less than 2.0). The hospital has cardiothoracic surgery with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capability on site and the perfusion team has been alerted.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation; oesophageal temperature 27.4 degrees Celsius; end tidal carbon dioxide 14 mmHg during compressions
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive, intubated with good bilateral chest rise; clothing removed and patient being dried; no evidence of major trauma
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); glucose 6.2 mmol/L; lactate 7 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue compressions while rewarming with warmed intravenous fluid and forced air blankets, and cease efforts if there is no response in thirty minutes
Cease resuscitation, since an end tidal carbon dioxide of 14 mmHg and a lactate of 7 mmol/L indicate futility in a prolonged arrest
Give intravenous amiodarone 300 mg and magnesium sulfate 10 mmol, then repeat defibrillation at two minute intervals
Continue compressions, withhold further shocks and adrenaline for now, and transfer him for extracorporeal rewarming
Deliver repeated stacked shocks at maximum energy and give adrenaline 1 mg every three to five minutes as per the standard algorithm

subtopic_detail: bradycardia and hyperkalaemia after new drugs reduced the clearance of a long standing rate control agent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 78-year-old woman brought in with five days of nausea, loss of appetite and increasing lethargy. She has atrial fibrillation and heart failure and has taken digoxin 125 micrograms daily and furosemide for six years.

Two weeks ago another doctor added perindopril and spironolactone after an outpatient echocardiogram. She has vomited twice today and says everything looks washed out and yellowish. Her monitor shows a slow regular ventricular rate despite her known atrial fibrillation, and her blood results are below. She takes no other new medication and has no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 42/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 5.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 165 micromol/L (45-90, was 88 three months ago), digoxin 3.8 nmol/L (0.6-1.3), magnesium 0.78 mmol/L (0.70-1.10)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Regularised slow ventricular response with downsloping ST depression in the lateral leads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate for the raised potassium immediately
Give insulin with dextrose and salbutamol, and recheck the potassium level
Give digoxin immune Fab and withhold all further doses of the drug
Arrange urgent haemodialysis to clear the drug and the potassium load
Insert a temporary pacing wire and observe without any specific antidote

subtopic_detail: hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia that will not correct despite replacement in a patient on long term acid suppression
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man admitted three days ago with cramps in his hands and feet and tingling around his mouth. He has taken pantoprazole 40 mg daily for six years for reflux.

He has received oral and intravenous potassium for three days and his potassium has barely moved. Tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the upper lip, and inflating the blood pressure cuff for two minutes produces carpal spasm. He is not vomiting, has no diarrhoea, takes no diuretic or laxative, and drinks alcohol twice a month. His blood pressure is normal and he is not alkalotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, no carpopedal deformity at rest, normal tone and power
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) after three days of replacement, corrected calcium 1.92 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), magnesium 0.38 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 1.0 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), parathyroid hormone at the lower end of the reference range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the potassium replacement and recheck the level in the morning
Give intravenous calcium gluconate alone and repeat the calcium later
Start calcitriol and oral calcium carbonate for the low calcium level now
Give intravenous magnesium and stop the proton pump inhibitor as well
Start spironolactone to reduce the ongoing urinary potassium wasting

subtopic_detail: lymphocytic exudative effusion with nodular pleural thickening and two negative cytology samples
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 68-year-old retired carpenter with three months of increasing breathlessness and a dull ache in the right side of his chest. He built and renovated houses from the mid 1970s and recalls cutting a great deal of fibre sheeting without a mask.

He has had two therapeutic aspirations of a large right pleural effusion in the last six weeks. Both fluid samples were exudative with a lymphocyte predominance, negative cultures including mycobacterial culture, and cytology reported as negative for malignant cells on each occasion. He has never smoked. Computed tomography today shows circumferential nodular pleural thickening extending onto the mediastinal pleura, with the effusion reaccumulating.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 48 g/L with serum protein 70 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase above two thirds the upper serum limit, lymphocyte predominant differential, cultures including mycobacterial culture negative, cytology negative on two samples
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography showing circumferential nodular pleural thickening involving the mediastinal pleura with a reaccumulating right effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pleural fluid cytology a third time before any further step
Start empirical antituberculous therapy for a lymphocytic exudate now
Arrange a positron emission tomography scan and review in four weeks
Start a trial of diuretics and repeat the chest radiograph in one month
Arrange image guided pleural biopsy to obtain tissue for histology

subtopic_detail: markedly elevated low density lipoprotein cholesterol with tendon thickening and premature coronary disease in a parent
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old man who came for a workplace health check. He has no symptoms, does not smoke, walks daily and drinks four standard drinks a week.

His fasting lipid profile has been repeated on two occasions eight weeks apart with consistent results. On examination both Achilles tendons feel thickened and nodular, and there are no xanthelasmata. His father had a myocardial infarction at 46 and his paternal grandmother died suddenly at 52. His blood pressure is 126/78 mmHg, his body mass index is 24 kg/m2, and he has two brothers and a 16-year-old daughter.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral Achilles tendon thickening with nodularity, no xanthelasmata, no corneal arcus
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 9.6 mmol/L (<5.5), low density lipoprotein cholesterol 7.4 mmol/L (<3.5), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L (>1.0), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (<1.7), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c 5.2 per cent (<6.0), liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a low dose statin and recheck the lipid profile in twelve months
Advise dietary change alone and repeat the lipid profile in six months
Start a high intensity statin and arrange cascade testing of relatives
Start ezetimibe alone and arrange a coronary calcium score this month
Refer for lipoprotein apheresis before starting any medical treatment

subtopic_detail: urethral discharge with intracellular Gram negative diplococci on the smear while nucleic acid testing is pending
stem:
You are the doctor in a sexual health clinic seeing a 24-year-old man with four days of burning on passing urine and a thick discharge that is staining his underwear.

He had condomless anal and oral sex with a new male partner ten days ago and has had two other partners in the last three months. He has no fever, no rash, no joint pain and no testicular pain. He takes no pre-exposure prophylaxis and his last testing was nine months ago and negative. A Gram stained smear of the urethral discharge taken in the clinic shows polymorphs containing Gram negative diplococci. Nucleic acid amplification testing on a first pass urine sample and on throat and rectal swabs has been sent and will take two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Purulent urethral discharge, no scrotal tenderness or swelling, no skin lesions, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urethral Gram stain showing intracellular Gram negative diplococci, nucleic acid amplification testing pending on urine and on throat and rectal swabs, serology for human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Give oral doxycycline for seven days and await the nucleic acid results
Give a single dose of oral azithromycin alone and review in one week
Await the nucleic acid results before starting any antibiotic treatment
Give ceftriaxone with azithromycin now and arrange partner notification
Give oral ciprofloxacin as a single dose and repeat the testing in a week

subtopic_detail: symmetrical polyarthralgia with a rash after mosquito exposure on an inland river camping trip
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old warehouse supervisor with ten days of pain and stiffness in both wrists, both ankles and both knees. She says she is covered in bites from a camping trip along an inland river system three weeks ago, where mosquitoes were dreadful at dusk.

The stiffness is worst for the first hour of the morning and the fatigue is profound enough that she has taken a week off work. A blotchy pink rash appeared over her trunk and arms four days ago and is fading. She has no fever now, though she felt hot and shivery in the first few days. She has no tick bite or eschar, no genital or eye symptoms, no recent diarrhoea and no overseas travel in the last two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical tenderness of wrists, ankles and knees with mild soft tissue swelling and no large effusions, fading maculopapular rash on trunk and arms, no eschar or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (<5), creatinine and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start prednisolone 25 mg daily for two weeks and review the joints then
Start doxycycline for a presumed tick borne infection and review in a week
Refer for urgent joint aspiration of both wrists to exclude sepsis today
Start methotrexate for probable early inflammatory arthritis this month
Send arbovirus serology and manage with analgesia and graded activity

subtopic_detail: high anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal blood glucose after several days of vomiting and no oral intake
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 44-year-old man with three days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has drunk a bottle of spirits most days for 15 years, drank heavily until four days ago, and has eaten almost nothing since.

He is tremulous with a mild tachycardia and is breathing deeply. His abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding. He has no fever, no melaena and no jaundice. His blood alcohol concentration is undetectable and his lipase is normal. He has never been diagnosed with diabetes and his HbA1c is 4.9 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.24 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32), anion gap 24 mmol/L (8-16), glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L (<0.6), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), blood alcohol undetectable, lipase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give intravenous saline with glucose plus thiamine and replace potassium
Start an intravenous insulin infusion with fluid at the usual protocol rates
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis now
Give intravenous saline alone and recheck the ketones in eight hours
Arrange urgent haemodialysis for a severe high anion gap acidosis today

subtopic_detail: seizure then a broad complex bradyarrhythmia minutes after a large volume regional block
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. You have just performed an ultrasound guided fascia iliaca block with a large volume of ropivacaine for a 58-year-old woman with a fractured neck of femur, after negative aspiration at each step.

Eight minutes later she complains that her lips feel numb and there is a metallic taste in her mouth, then becomes agitated and says the room sounds strange. Two minutes after that she has a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, terminated with intravenous midazolam. Her monitor now shows a broad complex rhythm at 38 beats per minute with a systolic pressure of 68 mmHg. The resuscitation trolley and airway equipment are at the bedside and a second doctor is calling for help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38/min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 8/min with bag mask support, SpO2 93% on 15 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal with reduced conscious state, airway supported with a bag and mask, no external haemorrhage
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Broad complex bradycardia with QRS duration 180 ms and no discernible P waves

lead_in: What is the most important specific treatment to give now?

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil and prepare for immediate endotracheal intubation
Give intravenous lipid emulsion while continuing standard resuscitation measures
Give intravenous adrenaline at the standard 1 mg arrest dose immediately
Give intravenous amiodarone for the broad complex rhythm and observe her
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and repeat the dose after five minutes

subtopic_detail: exertional syncope in a young athlete with a murmur that increases on standing and lateral T wave inversion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old semi-professional footballer who blacked out twice in the last month, both times during sprinting at training. Each episode lasted under a minute with rapid full recovery and no confusion afterwards.

He has no chest pain and no palpitations, and he has never fainted while standing still or after standing up. His mother's brother died suddenly at 34 while jogging and no cause was found. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting and softer when he squats down. His electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge louder on standing from squatting and softer on squatting, brisk carotid upstroke, no radiation to the carotids
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in leads V5, V6, I and aVL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that exertional syncope in young athletes is usually benign
Arrange an exercise stress test to reproduce the symptoms before imaging
Arrange transthoracic echocardiography and withhold competitive sport now
Start a beta blocker and allow training to continue while awaiting review
Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor alone and review the result in one month

subtopic_detail: progressive breathlessness with a large inspiratory fall in systolic pressure and low voltage complexes in advanced malignancy
stem:
You are the oncology registrar called to see a 64-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma who has become breathless over five days and cannot lie flat.

She is sitting forward and is anxious. Her jugular venous pressure is visible at the angle of the jaw at 45 degrees and rises further on inspiration. Her heart sounds are quiet and her chest is clear on auscultation with no crackles. Measuring her blood pressure carefully, the systolic falls by 16 mmHg during inspiration. Her electrocardiogram shows small complexes throughout with beat to beat variation in QRS amplitude, and her chest radiograph shows an enlarged globular cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. A bedside echocardiogram shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated and rising on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, chest clear on auscultation, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram with low voltage complexes and beat to beat QRS amplitude variation, chest radiograph with globular cardiac silhouette and clear lung fields, echocardiogram with large circumferential pericardial effusion and diastolic right atrial collapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg and reassess the breathlessness later
Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion to reduce the pulmonary congestion
Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange radiotherapy for the tumour
Arrange urgent echocardiography guided pericardiocentesis and drainage
Arrange computed tomography of the chest before any further treatment

subtopic_detail: headache and nausea in several members of a household that improve away from home, with normal pulse oximetry
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 35-year-old woman with three days of throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness. It is the middle of a cold winter.

She tells you that both of her housemates have the same headache and one vomited this morning, and that all three feel better by the middle of the day at work and worse again a few hours after they get home. Their unflued gas heater in the living room has been running each evening since the cold weather started, and one housemate noticed sooty marks on the wall above it. She has no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no rash and no fever. Her neurological examination is normal and her pulse oximeter reads 99 per cent in room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, no neck stiffness or photophobia, normal fundoscopy, normal neurological examination, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and metoclopramide for a presumed viral illness
Arrange computed tomography of the brain before any specific treatment
Give sumatriptan and advise review if the headaches persist next week
Arrange lumbar puncture after imaging to exclude subarachnoid bleeding
Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and take a blood gas sample

subtopic_detail: day three assessment of response to intravenous corticosteroid in an acute severe colitis admission
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman on day three of an admission with ulcerative colitis. She came in with nine bloody stools a day, cramping and fatigue, and has been on intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission.

Today she reports seven bloody stools in the last 24 hours, including two overnight. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness and no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens is negative, and sigmoidoscopy on admission showed deep ulceration without cytomegalovirus inclusions on biopsy. Her abdominal radiograph today shows a transverse colon diameter of 4 cm with no free gas. She has had no previous biologic therapy and her tuberculosis and hepatitis screening sent on admission are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 52 mg/L (<5, was 68 on admission), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), stool testing negative for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens, transverse colon diameter 4 cm on abdominal radiograph
data_table.Medications: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission, enoxaparin prophylaxis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start rescue therapy with infliximab and involve the colorectal surgeons
Continue intravenous corticosteroid for a further five days and reassess
Switch to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and plan discharge in two days
Start oral mesalazine at maximal dose and continue the corticosteroid
Start oral loperamide to reduce stool frequency and continue the steroid

subtopic_detail: confusion in an older woman with a near normal pH concealing a high anion gap acidosis and a respiratory alkalosis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 72-year-old woman brought in by her son with four days of increasing confusion. He says she has been complaining that her ears are ringing and has been breathing oddly since yesterday.

She takes aspirin 300 mg four times daily, bought over the counter for shoulder pain, and her son thinks she has also been taking a powder from the chemist for the same pain. She is agitated, disoriented to time and place, sweaty and febrile at 38.1 °C, with deep rapid respirations. Her chest is clear, there is no neck stiffness or rash, and her neurological examination shows no focal deficit. She has taken no deliberate overdose according to her son, and her regular tablets are all accounted for.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 38.1 °C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.41 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 22 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), anion gap 22 mmol/L (8-16), sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110), salicylate 3.9 mmol/L (therapeutic 1.1-2.2)

Give sodium bicarbonate with potassium and arrange urgent haemodialysis
Intubate and ventilate for airway protection given her confusion now
Give intravenous fluid alone and monitor her conscious state closely

subtopic_detail: a shuffling wide based gait preceding urinary urgency and mental slowing with enlarged ventricles
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 76-year-old man whose daughter says his walking has changed over about nine months. She describes his feet as looking stuck to the floor when he sets off and when he turns in the hallway, and says he takes several small steps to get around a corner.

The walking came first. Over the past three months he has begun rushing to the toilet and has twice not made it, and in the last month she has noticed he is slower to answer questions and has stopped doing the crossword. On examination his stride is short and his feet are wide apart, and he takes six steps to turn 180 degrees. There is no tremor at rest, no bradykinesia of repetitive finger tapping, no cogwheel rigidity and no asymmetry of limb tone. Power, reflexes and sensation are normal and the plantar responses are flexor. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 23 out of 30, losing points on attention and executive tasks with preserved delayed recall. Computed tomography shows enlarged lateral ventricles disproportionate to the degree of cortical sulcal widening.

data_table.Gait: Short stride with a wide base, hesitation on initiation, six steps to turn 180 degrees
data_table.Symptom sequence: Gait disturbance for nine months, urinary urgency for three months, cognitive slowing for one month
data_table.Movement examination: No rest tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity or asymmetry of tone

Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review in two months
Perform a high volume lumbar puncture with gait testing before and after
Start levodopa and assess the gait response after six weeks of treatment
Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up

subtopic_detail: fever ten days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count below half a billion per litre
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 58-year-old woman who finished her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer ten days ago. She has felt shivery since this morning and recorded a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius at home.

She has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash. Her central venous access device site is clean with no erythema, tenderness or discharge. On examination her chest is clear, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and the mouth shows no ulceration or thrush. Her pulse rate is 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Her white cell count is 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and C-reactive protein 94 mg/L (less than 5).

subtopic_detail: strictly unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation and agitation in nightly attacks lasting an hour
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who has come in at two in the morning with severe pain behind his right eye. He says it has woken him about ninety minutes after falling asleep every night for the past eighteen days, lasts around an hour and then goes completely.

He cannot sit still during the attack and paces the cubicle, rocking and pressing his palm into the socket, and tells you he would rather be doing anything than lying down. His right eye is watering and red, the right nostril is running, and the right upper lid is drooping with a smaller pupil on that side. There is no photophobia, no phonophobia and no vomiting, and he says he has been completely well between attacks and has kept working. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks a beer most evenings, which he has noticed now sets off an attack. Neurological examination including fundoscopy is otherwise normal and he is afebrile with no neck stiffness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits

data_table.Behaviour in attack: Restless and pacing, unable to lie still
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundoscopy, no neck stiffness, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate acute treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral sumatriptan to be taken at the onset of each further attack
Start carbamazepine and titrate the dose against the attack frequency
Prescribe regular oral prednisolone for the duration of the current cluster
Start propranolol as preventive treatment and review him in eight weeks
Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan

subtopic_detail: a rising creatinine during a diarrhoeal illness in a woman taking three drugs that each impair renal autoregulation
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72-year-old woman three days into a diarrhoeal illness that her whole family has had. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis, and takes perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen, the last of which she buys herself and has been taking regularly for knee pain.

She has kept drinking cordial but has passed urine only twice today. On examination her mucous membranes are dry, the jugular venous pressure is not visible, and there is a postural drop from 128/74 mmHg lying to 104/62 mmHg standing with a pulse rate of 96 beats per minute. There is no rash, no fever, no loin tenderness and no palpable bladder. Creatinine is 186 micromol/L (45-90), up from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), potassium 5.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) and sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145). Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes, and microscopy shows no casts, no eosinophils and no crystals. A renal tract ultrasound reports normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not visible, no rash, no loin tenderness, no palpable bladder
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90) from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0)

data_table.Imaging: Normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis

options.text: Withhold the perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen and rehydrate her
Withhold the perindopril only and continue the other two medications
Start prednisolone for a presumed acute interstitial nephritis today
Insert a urinary catheter and arrange renal tract imaging this evening
Refer for urgent renal biopsy to establish the underlying diagnosis

subtopic_detail: a falling phosphate on the third day of nutritional support after a fortnight of minimal oral intake
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man admitted eight days ago after a fall at home, where he had been living alone and eating almost nothing for a fortnight because of low mood after his wife died. He weighs 48 kg and his body mass index is 16.2 kg/m2.

Nasogastric feeding was started three days ago at his full estimated energy requirement. This morning he is more short of breath than yesterday, has new peripheral oedema and says his legs feel weak going to the toilet. On examination there are bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. His pulse rate is 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Phosphate is 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), having been 0.82 mmol/L on admission, potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.26 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110). His thiamine status was not assessed before feeding began.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure, new peripheral oedema, proximal weakness
data_table.Nutritional status: Weight 48 kg, body mass index 16.2 kg/m2, minimal oral intake for a fortnight before admission

data_table.Feeding history: Nasogastric feeding at full estimated requirement from day three of admission, thiamine status not assessed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to parenteral nutrition and add an insulin infusion for tight control
Reduce the feeding rate, replace phosphate intravenously and give thiamine

Stop feeding entirely and recommence once the phosphate has normalised

subtopic_detail: excessive daytime sleepiness with witnessed apnoeas in a heavy vehicle driver awaiting a sleep study
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who drives a semi-trailer on overnight interstate runs. He has come for a repeat prescription and mentions that he nodded off at the wheel for a moment approaching a roundabout last week and put it down to a long shift.

His partner says he snores loudly, stops breathing and then gasps several times a night. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. His body mass index is 37 kg/m2, his neck circumference is 45 cm and his blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg on two occasions despite perindopril. He has fallen asleep watching television and while sitting in the waiting room today. Examination shows a crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields and no peripheral oedema, and his oxygen saturation is 95 per cent in air. A polysomnogram has been requested and the next available appointment in the public system is in fourteen weeks. He asks you to sign his commercial driving medical certificate today.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 152/94 mmHg on two occasions, SpO2 95 per cent in air, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Sleep history: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas and gasping, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 17 out of 24

data_table.Examination: Crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Pending investigation: Polysomnogram requested with a fourteen week wait

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Start modafinil to control the sleepiness while he awaits the sleep study
Refer for bariatric surgery assessment and continue his current work duties
Advise him to stop commercial driving now and document that advice clearly
Allow him to keep driving until the sleep study result becomes available

subtopic_detail: recurrent oral and genital ulceration with blurred vision and a positive skin prick response
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 29-year-old man born in Turkey who has had crops of painful mouth ulcers for three years, occurring six or seven times a year and taking a fortnight to heal. Over the past year he has also had two episodes of painful scrotal ulceration that left scars.

He now reports three days of blurred vision and floaters in the right eye with some aching around it. On examination there are four shallow ulcers with erythematous rims on the buccal mucosa and two healed scars on the scrotum, and there are several tender erythematous nodules on both shins. A cannula inserted in the emergency department yesterday has developed a sterile pustule at the puncture site. Herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction from an ulcer base is negative, coeliac serology is negative, and his full blood count, iron studies, B12 and folate are all normal. C-reactive protein is 42 mg/L (less than 5) and he is afebrile with otherwise normal vital signs.

data_table.Mucocutaneous findings: Four shallow buccal ulcers with erythematous rims, two healed scrotal scars, tender erythematous nodules on both shins

subtopic_detail: progressive headache with papilloedema and a focal seizure in a woman taking combined oral contraception
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 31-year-old woman with eight days of headache that has become steadily worse. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and returned from a long-haul flight a fortnight ago.

She describes the headache as a constant band that is worse when she lies flat, worse when she coughs or strains, and worst on waking. This afternoon her left arm jerked rhythmically for about ninety seconds while she remained aware throughout, and afterwards the arm felt weak for twenty minutes. On examination there is bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, and visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye. Power, tone, reflexes and sensation are now normal in all four limbs and she is fully oriented. There is no neck stiffness, no fever and no rash. An unenhanced computed tomography scan of the brain shows a small area of haemorrhage in the right parietal region with surrounding low attenuation that does not conform to an arterial territory. Her vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Headache pattern: Eight days of progressive headache worse lying flat, on coughing and straining, and on waking
data_table.Seizure: Focal motor seizure of the left arm lasting 90 seconds with retained awareness and 20 minutes of postictal weakness
data_table.Fundoscopy: Bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally

options.text: Arrange venographic imaging and start therapeutic anticoagulation
Withhold anticoagulation because of the intracranial haemorrhage present
Start intravenous mannitol and refer for decompressive craniectomy now
Load with levetiracetam and repeat the unenhanced scan in 24 hours
Start high dose aspirin and arrange carotid duplex ultrasound tomorrow

subtopic_detail: new back pain with brisk lower limb reflexes and a sensory level in a man with known metastatic disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department at ten at night to see a 71-year-old man with prostate cancer and known bone metastases, on androgen deprivation therapy. He has had mid back pain for three weeks that is worse lying flat and wakes him, and today he has found the stairs difficult and nearly fell twice.

He says his legs feel heavy rather than painful and that he has had to strain to start passing urine since yesterday. On examination hip flexion is 4 out of 5 bilaterally with normal power in the arms, both knee and ankle reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus, and both plantar responses are extensor. There is a band of reduced pinprick sensation below the level of the umbilicus. The bladder is palpable to three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. There is percussion tenderness over the mid thoracic spine. His observations are normal, his prostate specific antigen has risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, and his corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55).

data_table.Reflexes and tone: Brisk knee and ankle reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, extensor plantar responses bilaterally

data_table.Other findings: Palpable bladder three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis, mid thoracic percussion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Prostate specific antigen risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine within the next week
Give high dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent whole spine imaging
Arrange a plain radiograph of the lumbar spine and review the result first
Start opioid analgesia and refer to outpatient radiation oncology clinic
Arrange a radionuclide bone scan and refer for palliative radiotherapy later

subtopic_detail: a platelet fall of more than half on day seven of low molecular weight heparin with a new limb thrombosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 66-year-old woman who is day seven after an elective total knee replacement and has been on prophylactic enoxaparin since the operation. The nursing staff have called you because her left calf has become swollen and painful overnight.

On examination the left calf is 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins, and the surgical wound is clean and dry with no erythema or discharge. There is no bleeding from the wound, no bruising and no petechiae anywhere. Her platelet count is 68 x10^9/L today, having been 198 x10^9/L on the day of surgery and 186 x10^9/L on day three. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115-155), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), fibrinogen 4.1 g/L (2.0-4.0), prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are both normal and the blood film shows no schistocytes and no platelet clumping. Compression ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Her temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and the remaining vital signs are normal.

data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and deep venous tenderness, clean dry surgical wound, no bleeding, bruising or petechiae

data_table.Imaging: Compression ultrasound showing occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein

Continue enoxaparin and give intravenous immunoglobulin for the low count

subtopic_detail: tender shin nodules with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle arthritis in a woman of thirty
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman referred after a chest radiograph taken for two weeks of ankle pain and swelling. She has crops of tender red raised lumps over both shins that came up ten days ago.

She has had no cough, no breathlessness on climbing two flights, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss. She was born in Australia, has not travelled overseas, and has had no known contact with anyone with tuberculosis. On examination there are six tender erythematous nodules on both shins, both ankles are warm and swollen with painful dorsiflexion, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no lymphadenopathy palpable in the neck, axillae or groins, and there are no skin lesions elsewhere, no red eye and no facial rash. The chest radiograph shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. An interferon gamma release assay is negative, corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), and her spirometry and gas transfer are normal.

data_table.Skin examination: Six tender erythematous nodules over both shins present for ten days

options.text: Start standard four drug antituberculous therapy while cultures are awaited
Start high dose oral prednisolone and taper it over the next six months

Treat symptomatically with a nonsteroidal drug and review her in six weeks
Arrange endobronchial ultrasound guided lymph node sampling within the week

subtopic_detail: a rising urate and potassium after induction chemotherapy in a man whose brother haemolysed on primaquine
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 34-year-old man received the first dose of induction chemotherapy for a bulky high grade lymphoma fourteen hours ago and has been on intravenous fluids with allopurinol since admission. He feels nauseated and has cramp in both hands but is otherwise comfortable.

His family came to Australia from Sardinia. He tells you his older brother was admitted with dark urine and jaundice after taking an antimalarial before a trip, and that he was told to avoid the same tablet and fava beans. He has never been tested himself. On examination he has a positive Trousseau sign and is otherwise unremarkable. His pulse rate is 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Potassium is 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urate 0.68 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), phosphate 2.4 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), corrected calcium 1.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) from 82 micromol/L on admission and lactate dehydrogenase 1840 units/L (120-250). His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology and a QRS duration of 88 milliseconds. Urine output has been 30 mL per hour for the last three hours.

subtopic_detail: worsening hand shake in a man whose mood medication was increased three months before the tremor began
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 61-year-old man with a worsening hand tremor. He has spilled his tea twice this week and is embarrassed signing documents at the bank. He tells you the shaking started about six months ago and has become steadily more noticeable.

He has bipolar disorder that has been stable for years, and his sodium valproate was increased from 1000 mg to 1500 mg daily nine months ago after a brief hypomanic episode. He also takes perindopril. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and says alcohol makes no difference to the shaking. There is no family history of tremor. On examination there is a symmetrical fine tremor of both outstretched hands that is present throughout finger to nose movement and absent at rest. There is no rigidity, no bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, no reduction in arm swing and no facial masking. Gait is normal, and there is no head tremor or vocal tremor. Thyroid function and a serum valproate level are within their reference ranges.

subtopic_detail: widespread scaly oval trunk rash also involving both palms and soles in a young man
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old man with a rash that appeared ten days ago and has spread across his trunk. He is not particularly itchy. He had a mild sore throat and felt tired for a few days beforehand.

He assumed it was a viral rash and has been using a moisturiser. He is otherwise well with no fever now. On examination there are multiple oval salmon pink scaly macules and papules 5 to 15 mm across scattered over the trunk, with the long axis of the lesions following the skin lines over the back. There are similar scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and both soles, and a few on the shaft of the penis. There is no single larger patch preceding the eruption that he can recall. He has non-tender rubbery lymph nodes palpable in both axillae and both groins, and there are a few small moth eaten patches of hair loss on the occipital scalp. He has had four male sexual partners in the past year and last tested for sexually transmitted infections two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Oval salmon pink scaly papules over the trunk following skin lines, scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and soles, papules on the penile shaft
data_table.Lymph nodes: Non-tender rubbery generalised lymphadenopathy in both axillae and both groins

subtopic_detail: night time hand tingling with flattening of the muscle bulk at the base of the thumb
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 57-year-old cleaner with eighteen months of tingling in her right hand that wakes her most nights and is relieved by shaking the hand over the side of the bed. She has recently started dropping cups and cannot reliably do up buttons or turn a key.

She was given a wrist splint by a physiotherapist a year ago and wore it nightly for three months with some early benefit that has since been lost. She has no neck pain and no pain radiating from the neck. She has no diabetes and thyroid function tested last month was normal. On examination there is visible flattening of the muscle bulk over the ball of the thumb on the right compared with the left, and thumb abduction against resistance is weak on the right. Sensation is reduced to light touch over the palmar surfaces of the thumb, index and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the little finger and over the skin at the base of the thumb. Neck movements are full and painless, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Visible right thenar wasting with weak thumb abduction against resistance, normal bulk on the left
data_table.Sensory findings: Reduced light touch over the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers, spared little finger and spared thenar eminence skin

Refit a neutral position night wrist splint and arrange a review of her symptoms in three months

subtopic_detail: painful stiff shoulder in a woman whose passive external rotation is as restricted as her active movement
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53-year-old woman with six months of right shoulder pain. It began without injury, was worst at night for the first three months and woke her whenever she rolled onto that side, and the night pain has now eased while the stiffness has become the dominant problem.

She can no longer reach behind her back to fasten a bra or reach up to a high cupboard. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and her most recent glycated haemoglobin was 8.4 per cent (target under 7.0). On examination active abduction is limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees. When you relax her arm and move it passively, external rotation remains restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point and reproduces her pain. There is no tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint and no painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees. Power in the rotator cuff muscles is preserved within the available range, and a radiograph of the shoulder shows no calcification, no fracture and preserved joint space.

data_table.Examination: Active abduction limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees
data_table.Passive movement: Passive external rotation equally restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point, reproducing the pain
data_table.Other findings: No acromioclavicular tenderness, no painful arc, rotator cuff power preserved within the available range

subtopic_detail: continuous spinning for eighteen hours with a normal head impulse test and a normal early brain scan
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 63-year-old man who woke yesterday evening with the room spinning and has been continuously dizzy since, unable to stand without help and vomiting repeatedly. He has hypertension and smokes fifteen cigarettes a day.

He has had no hearing loss, no tinnitus and no headache, and he reports no double vision, no slurred speech and no limb weakness. On examination he is distressed and pale but alert and fully oriented. There is horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the left when he looks ahead, which reverses direction and beats to the right when he looks to the right. Horizontal head impulse testing produces no corrective saccade in either direction. Alternate cover testing shows a small vertical realignment of the right eye. Limb power, tone and reflexes are normal and there is no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, but he cannot sit unsupported on the trolley without falling to the left. A non contrast computed tomography scan of the brain performed an hour ago is reported as normal.

data_table.Eye movements: Horizontal nystagmus beating left in primary gaze that reverses to beat right on right gaze, small vertical realignment of the right eye on alternate cover testing
data_table.Head impulse test: No corrective saccade on rapid horizontal head impulse in either direction
data_table.Neurological: Normal limb power, tone and reflexes, no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, unable to sit unsupported without falling to the left
data_table.Imaging: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

Arrange outpatient audiometry and a carotid duplex ultrasound with review in the next week
Give intravenous prochlorperazine, rehydrate him and reassess his symptoms in four hours
Commence a tapering course of oral prednisolone and refer him for vestibular rehabilitation

subtopic_detail: man with a drooping face who cannot raise the eyebrow on the affected side and cannot close that eye
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old carpenter who woke yesterday morning with the right side of his face not working. He noticed coffee dribbling from the corner of his mouth and his wife said his face looked crooked. He had noticed some pain behind the right ear the day before.

He says sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the right ear and that food tastes odd. He has had no fever, no rash, no headache, no limb weakness and no difficulty speaking or swallowing. He has not travelled outside Australia and has no tick exposure. On examination the right side of the face is weak throughout: he cannot wrinkle the right forehead, cannot fully close the right eye, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Power and reflexes are normal in all four limbs, the pupils are equal and reactive and eye movements are full. The external auditory canal and the tympanic membrane are normal with no vesicles, and the parotid region is normal on palpation.

data_table.Ear and parotid: Normal external auditory canal and tympanic membrane with no vesicles, normal parotid on palpation

subtopic_detail: acutely hot swollen first toe joint in a man whose kidney function is severely reduced
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 66-year-old man who woke at 3 am with an exquisitely painful right great toe. He cannot bear the weight of the bedsheet on it. He has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each resolving over a week.

He has stage 4 chronic kidney disease from long standing hypertension and takes perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He is not on a diuretic and takes no anticoagulant. He has no history of peptic ulcer disease, diabetes or heart failure. On examination he is afebrile and systemically well. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot, swollen and exquisitely tender with overlying shiny skin, and there is no break in the skin and no ascending erythema or lymphangitis. No other joint is involved. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 square metres, creatinine 248 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum urate 0.54 mmol/L (0.20 to 0.42), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5) and white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0).

subtopic_detail: older woman with an acutely swollen knee and a thin white line in the joint cartilage on radiograph
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman admitted yesterday for management of community-acquired pneumonia, who has developed a painful swollen left knee overnight. She is on day two of intravenous benzylpenicillin and is improving from a respiratory point of view.

She has had no previous joint problems, no recent injury and no prosthetic joints. She takes no anticoagulant. On examination she is alert with a temperature of 37.8 degrees. The left knee is warm, swollen with a demonstrable effusion, and painful through the last 20 degrees of flexion, though she can straight leg raise. There is no overlying skin break, no rash and no other joint involvement. A plain radiograph of the knee shows a fine linear opacity within the meniscal cartilage and within the hyaline cartilage of both femoral condyles, with moderate joint space narrowing. C reactive protein is 88 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) and serum urate is 0.28 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.40).

subtopic_detail: shallow ulcer above the inner ankle with brown staining that improves when the leg is raised
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 69-year-old retired nurse with an ulcer on her left lower leg that has been present for four months. It aches by the end of the day and the ache eases when she puts her feet up on the lounge in the evening.

She stood for long shifts for thirty years and has varicose veins on both legs. She has hypertension and a body mass index of 31 kg per square metre, and she has never smoked and has no diabetes. On examination there is a shallow ulcer 4 cm across with a sloping edge and a granulating base just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown stained with pitting oedema and firm inelastic skin over the lower third of the calf. The foot is warm and pink with normal capillary refill, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are both palpable. Monofilament sensation is intact at all sites. The ankle brachial pressure index is 1.0 on the affected side.

subtopic_detail: thickened crumbling discolouration of several toenails in a man who wants treatment before a holiday
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old man who is embarrassed about his toenails and wants them treated before a beach holiday. Over about three years the nails have become thickened, yellow brown and crumbly, and the first, third and fourth toenails on the right foot and the first on the left are affected.

He has no diabetes, no peripheral vascular symptoms and takes no regular medications. He plays squash twice a week and uses communal changing rooms. On examination the affected nails are thickened with subungual debris lifting the nail plate from the bed at the free edge, and the discolouration runs from the distal edge proximally. There is fine scaling in the fourth toe web spaces bilaterally. The unaffected nails are normal, there is no nail pitting, no oil drop sign and no skin plaques at the elbows, knees or scalp. Pedal pulses are palpable, the feet are warm and monofilament sensation is intact.

subtopic_detail: woman with central facial flushing and papules whose eyes are gritty with crusted lid margins
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old woman with two years of facial redness that she has treated as sensitive skin. She flushes with red wine, hot drinks and stepping into a warm room, and over the past six months small red bumps have appeared across her cheeks and nose.

She has used a topical corticosteroid cream prescribed for eczema intermittently over the past year, which helps for a few days before the redness returns worse. She also mentions that her eyes have felt gritty and dry for months and that her eyelids are crusted in the mornings. On examination there is persistent erythema with telangiectasia across the cheeks, nose and chin, with scattered papules and pustules and no comedones. The eyelid margins are thickened and erythematous with crusting at the lash bases, and the conjunctivae are mildly injected. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining.

subtopic_detail: recurrent hours long spinning with fluctuating low frequency hearing loss and ear fullness on one side
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old woman with recurrent attacks of the room spinning. Over the past eight months she has had six episodes, each building over minutes, lasting three to four hours, and leaving her unsteady for a day afterwards. She vomits during them and has to lie still in a dark room.

She describes a sense of pressure and fullness in the left ear before and during each attack, with a low pitched roaring noise on that side, and says her hearing in that ear is muffled during an attack and improves between episodes. She has no headache with the attacks, no photophobia or visual aura, and no history of migraine. There is no positional trigger and the attacks come without warning. Between attacks her examination is normal with no nystagmus, normal gait and a negative head impulse test bilaterally. Weber lateralises to the right and Rinne is positive bilaterally. A pure tone audiogram taken last week shows a 35 decibel sensorineural loss at 250 and 500 Hz on the left with normal thresholds above 2000 Hz.

subtopic_detail: daily itchy weals for five months resolving within a day each and no response to a standard antihistamine dose
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman with itchy raised weals that have appeared almost every day for five months. Individual weals come up on the trunk and limbs, are intensely itchy, and fade completely within about twelve hours leaving no mark behind.

She has been taking cetirizine 10 mg once daily for three months with only partial benefit and is losing sleep. She has identified no food, drug or physical trigger, and the weals appear at rest as often as with exercise. She has had no lip, tongue or throat swelling, no abdominal pain and no breathing difficulty. She takes no other medications including no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. On examination there are scattered pink weals of varying size on the trunk and thighs, each blanching on pressure, with no purpura, no residual pigmentation and no scaling. There is no wheeze, the joints are not swollen, and she is afebrile with no weight loss. Full blood examination, C reactive protein and thyroid function are within normal limits.

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a post enteric inflammatory arthritis from septic arthritis when the synovial white cell count is raised
stem:

Three weeks ago he had five days of profuse watery diarrhoea after a camping trip with friends, which settled without treatment. For the past five days his right knee has been swollen and painful and his left ankle has become sore, and this morning he could not put his heel to the ground.

He also describes both eyes being red and gritty for a week and pain where the back of his heel meets the bone. He injects no drugs, has no skin breaks and no indwelling lines. You aspirate the knee at the bedside and send the fluid urgently. The aspirate results return while he is still in the department.

subtopic_detail: acting on a frailty assessment rather than chronological age before major elective surgery
stem:

She lives alone in a unit and uses a four wheeled frame indoors. Her daughter does her shopping and manages her medicines in a dose administration aid, and she has stopped going to her weekly card group because she tires. She has lost 6 kg over the past year without trying. She tells you she wants to do whatever will let her stay in her own home. Her cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable and her recent bloods are unremarkable.

subtopic_detail: prioritising which medicine to withdraw first after recurrent falls when there is no postural drop
stem:

His daughter has brought in his dose administration aid. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, temazepam nightly which he has taken for about six years, sertraline, aspirin, atorvastatin, metformin, pantoprazole, docusate and regular paracetamol. He drinks no alcohol. Lying and standing blood pressures have been recorded on the ward over two days.

subtopic_detail: changing opioid and route when the oral route fails and renal function is deteriorating at the end of life
stem:

Over the past three days she has vomited after most doses and has not reliably kept a tablet down. Her husband says she has become much drowsier and that her hands and arms twitch in short jerks when she dozes, which is new. Bloods were taken yesterday by the visiting nurse. subtopic_detail: choosing the starting corticosteroid dose for girdle pain when cranial arteritis features are absent

She has taken atorvastatin for three years without previous problems. She has no jaw pain on chewing, no scalp tenderness and no visual symptoms, and her temporal arteries are not tender or thickened. There is no swelling of the small joints of her hands.

options.text: Commence prednisolone 15 mg daily and review the response in one week
Cease atorvastatin and review the symptoms in the clinic in six weeks
Commence prednisolone 50 mg daily and refer for temporal artery biopsy
Commence weekly methotrexate 10 mg with folic acid supplementation
Commence regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily and refer to physiotherapy

subtopic_detail: recognising sight threatening orbitopathy when the thyroid biochemistry has already been corrected
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman in the emergency department. She has been taking carbimazole for three months for hyperthyroidism and her most recent clinic bloods were reported as satisfactory.

For the past two weeks the vision in her right eye has been blurred, and this week she noticed that a red traffic light looks washed out and grey compared with how it appears through the left eye. She has forward protrusion of both eyes and cannot look up fully on the right. She is a current smoker of fifteen cigarettes daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, restricted elevation of the right eye, right relative afferent pupillary defect, red desaturation in the right eye, corneas intact
data_table.Investigations: Visual acuity 6/18 right and 6/6 left, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, free triiodothyronine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the carbimazole dose and review in the clinic in four weeks
Refer the same day for intravenous methylprednisolone under ophthalmology
Prescribe lubricant eye drops and review in the clinic in six weeks
Refer for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid within two weeks
Refer for routine orbital radiotherapy at the next available appointment

subtopic_detail: interpreting a normal random growth hormone in suspected somatotroph excess and choosing the screening test
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man referred with a two year history of headaches and increasing daytime sleepiness. A sleep study last year showed obstructive sleep apnoea and he uses continuous positive airway pressure.

He tells you that his wedding ring had to be cut off last year and that he has gone up three shoe sizes since his thirties. He has noticed new gaps appearing between his lower teeth and his dentist has remarked on the change in his bite. He has bilateral hand tingling that wakes him at night. His referring doctor has already sent one blood test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges, macroglossia, spade like hands, bilateral positive Tinel sign at the wrists, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Random serum growth hormone 1.8 mIU/L, glycated haemoglobin 7.2 per cent (less than 6.0), fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), calcium within normal limits, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the random serum growth hormone level on three separate mornings
Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements
Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched range
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast now
Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections

subtopic_detail: interpreting a markedly raised ferritin when the transferrin saturation is normal
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man who came in for a fatigue check. He works long hours, sleeps poorly and has gained weight steadily since his forties. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 112 cm.

He has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has done so for years. There is no family history of liver disease and no arthralgia, and he has no skin pigmentation change. His initial blood results have come back and his general practice colleague has flagged the ferritin.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 146/90, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no skin bronzing
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 980 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 31 per cent (15 to 45), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L (less than 35), C reactive protein within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send HFE genotyping for the C282Y and H63D variants before anything else
Begin weekly therapeutic venesection and recheck the ferritin at ten weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging for hepatic iron quantification now
Arrange liver ultrasound with viral serology and fasting iron studies
Refer for percutaneous liver biopsy to quantify the hepatic iron index

subtopic_detail: post exercise facilitation and autonomic features distinguishing a presynaptic neuromuscular disorder from myasthenia
stem:
You are the neurology registrar assessing a 63-year-old man referred with four months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily since he was twenty three.

He volunteers that his mouth has been persistently dry, that he has become constipated and that he has had difficulty with erections over the same period. He denies double vision and says his eyelids do not droop as the day goes on. On testing, his knee reflexes are absent, but after he holds a sustained quadriceps contraction for fifteen seconds they become obtainable, and his grip feels briefly stronger after repeated effort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 128/80 lying with a 14 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal lower limb weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes at rest which return after sustained contraction, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, dry oral mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, chest radiograph reported as no focal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies with repetitive nerve stimulation
Nerve conduction studies with a lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine with gadolinium contrast
Creatine kinase with electromyography and a subsequent muscle biopsy
Chest computed tomography with voltage gated calcium channel antibodies

subtopic_detail: screening for the diabetes of cystic fibrosis when the glycated haemoglobin is within normal limits
stem:
You are the registrar in the adult cystic fibrosis clinic reviewing a 24-year-old woman at her routine appointment. Her forced expiratory volume in one second is 62 per cent predicted and she has been established on modulator therapy for two years.

She has lost 4 kg over the past four months. She takes her pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack and her dietitian confirms her adherence and her intake have not changed. She has needed two courses of intravenous antibiotics for exacerbations in the past six months, up from none in the preceding year. She has noticed she is thirstier than usual but has not changed her diet.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19.1 kg/m2 down from 20.6 kg/m2 four months ago, scattered coarse crackles bilaterally, no clubbing change
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 5.9 per cent (less than 6.0), random plasma glucose 8.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), faecal elastase low consistent with known pancreatic insufficiency, liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Two hour 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test arranged in the next week
Repeat the glycated haemoglobin in three months and review the weight
Fasting plasma glucose on two separate mornings in the coming fortnight
Two weeks of continuous glucose monitoring with a clinic review after
Random plasma glucose with urinary ketones at the next clinic review

subtopic_detail: new mononeuritis multiplex with marked eosinophilia in a patient carrying an asthma label
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man in the emergency department. He has carried a diagnosis of asthma for six years, takes a high dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist, and has had nasal polyps removed twice.

Three weeks ago he developed a right foot drop that has not improved, and over the past week the ring and little fingers of his left hand have become numb and weak. He has a non blanching purple rash over both shins. He has not travelled overseas and has not started any new medication in the past year. His bloods and chest film are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right foot drop with weak ankle dorsiflexion, sensory loss in the left ulnar distribution with weak finger abduction, palpable purpura over both shins, expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 4.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 66 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine within normal limits, urinalysis within normal limits, troponin mildly raised
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral migratory infiltrates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate the inhaled therapy and add a monoclonal anti interleukin 5 agent
Commence high dose oral corticosteroid today with urgent specialist referral
Arrange nerve conduction studies and review in the clinic in six weeks
Send strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin before any steroid
Refer for skin prick allergy testing and commence a leukotriene antagonist

subtopic_detail: low voltage electrocardiogram with increased wall thickness and nephrotic range proteinuria in an infiltrative cardiomyopathy
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar assessing a 64-year-old man referred with five months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. He has lost 8 kg without trying and feels light headed whenever he stands up quickly.

His wife mentions that he has twice woken with purple marks around his eyes after a bout of coughing, and that his tongue looks bigger than it used to. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure has in fact been running lower than his usual over the past year, so his general practitioner stopped his only antihypertensive six months ago. There is no family history of cardiac disease or sudden death. His investigations are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/64 lying with a 28 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, macroglossia with lateral dental indentations, periorbital purpura
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 420 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35 to 50), estimated glomerular filtration rate 55 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide markedly raised, high sensitivity troponin persistently mildly raised without a rise and fall pattern
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with low voltage QRS complexes in the limb leads and poor R wave progression
data_table.Echocardiogram: Left ventricular wall thickness 16 mm, ejection fraction 52 per cent, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, biatrial enlargement, apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Technetium labelled bone scintigraphy to characterise the cardiac deposits
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement now
Serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation studies
Percutaneous renal biopsy to establish the cause of the proteinuria
Invasive coronary angiography to exclude an ischaemic cardiomyopathy

subtopic_detail: bilateral leg pain with a large post void residual and reduced perianal sensation five days after a lifting injury
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 42-year-old warehouse worker who developed severe low back pain five days ago while lifting a pallet. Over the past two days the pain has begun shooting down the back of both legs.

Since yesterday morning he has had to wait and strain to start passing urine and feels he never empties. This morning he noticed that the paper felt strange when he wiped himself. He has had no fevers, night sweats or weight loss, has never had cancer, uses no injected drugs and has no indwelling lines. His bowels last opened normally two days ago. A bladder scan in the department shows a post-void residual volume of 620 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over both buttocks and the perineum, reduced voluntary anal squeeze, ankle jerks absent bilaterally, power 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion on both sides, no spinal tenderness to percussion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine today
Computed tomography of the lumbar spine without intravenous contrast today
Intravenous dexamethasone commenced before any imaging is arranged for him
Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine in two planes including flexion views
Simple analgesia with physiotherapy and general practitioner review in one week

subtopic_detail: fixed airflow obstruction with lower zone predominant emphysema in a woman in her forties with a light smoking history
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 41-year-old primary school teacher referred with two years of breathlessness on exertion. She can no longer carry shopping up the stairs to her flat without stopping.

She smoked about five cigarettes a day for five years in her twenties and stopped eleven years ago. She has never worked in dusty or fume exposed environments, keeps no birds and has no mould in her home. She had no childhood asthma and uses no inhaler. Her brother died at forty five of liver failure that the family were told was cirrhosis without a cause being found. Her computed tomography shows emphysematous change concentrated in the lower zones of both lungs with relative sparing of the apices.
