data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, quiet breath sounds with prolonged expiration, no clubbing, no crackles, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in one second 48 per cent predicted, ratio to forced vital capacity 0.52, no significant bronchodilator response, diffusing capacity reduced, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase 88 U/L (less than 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the underlying cause?

options.text: Serum total immunoglobulin E with Aspergillus specific antibody testing
Serum alpha one antitrypsin concentration with phenotyping if it is reduced
Sweat chloride testing followed by an extended cystic fibrosis gene panel
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing with proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing with arterial blood gases taken at peak exercise

subtopic_detail: a magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild forgetfulness in an older man with ventriculomegaly and no parkinsonian signs
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 74-year-old retired surveyor referred after two falls at home in the past three months. His wife says he has changed over about eight months.

He describes his feet as feeling stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and has most trouble turning in the kitchen and getting going after standing. For the past three months he has had to rush to the toilet and has twice not made it. His wife says he repeats himself and has become slower in conversation, but he manages the household accounts and knows the date and where he is. There is no resting tremor, no rigidity and no reduction in the amplitude of repeated finger tapping. His posture is upright, his arm swing is preserved and there is no postural drop in blood pressure.

data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with reduced step height and difficulty turning, normal tone and power, Mini Mental State Examination 25 of 30, no tremor or rigidity, no postural hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the brain shows enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.38 and no disproportionate cortical atrophy, vitamin B12, thyroid stimulating hormone, syphilis serology, urea electrolytes and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound to assess for haemodynamically significant stenosis
Trial of levodopa titrated over six weeks with formal reassessment of his gait
High volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and afterwards
Referral for insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt on the imaging findings alone
Electroencephalography to exclude a non convulsive seizure disorder as the cause

subtopic_detail: confirming the haemodynamic diagnosis before treatment when echocardiography has already estimated a high right ventricular systolic pressure
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar seeing a 36-year-old woman with twelve months of breathlessness that has progressed from long walks to the distance between her car and her front door. Three weeks ago she blacked out briefly while carrying washing up a flight of stairs.

She has never smoked, takes no appetite suppressants and uses no stimulant drugs. She has no rash, no Raynaud phenomenon, no joint swelling and no dysphagia. She snores rarely and her partner has seen no pauses in her breathing. Her computed tomography pulmonary angiogram shows no filling defect and clear lung parenchyma, and a ventilation perfusion scan shows no mismatched defects. Her connective tissue serology and human immunodeficiency virus test are negative and her liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure raised 6 cm with a prominent v wave, loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, pitting oedema to mid shin
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram shows estimated right ventricular systolic pressure 68 mmHg with a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle, normal left ventricular function and structurally normal valves; spirometry normal with a reduced diffusing capacity; brain natriuretic peptide elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to assess for sleep disordered breathing as a cause
Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in six months to assess the rate of change
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium to assess the right ventricle
Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing in a specialist centre
Empirical sildenafil started now with reassessment of her exercise capacity later

subtopic_detail: a cord lesion spanning six vertebral segments with negative oligoclonal bands after an episode of painful visual loss
stem:
You are the neurology registrar admitting a 34-year-old woman with six days of progressive weakness in both legs, now unable to stand unaided, with a band of altered sensation across her trunk and difficulty passing urine.

Two months ago she had a painful right eye with loss of colour vision over several days, which recovered only partially, and she was told it was probably a viral problem. She has had no rash, no oral or genital ulceration, no dry eyes or mouth and no joint swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging of her spine shows a contiguous cord lesion extending from the fourth to the ninth thoracic vertebral level with swelling and patchy enhancement. Imaging of her brain shows no periventricular or juxtacortical lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 40 white cells per microlitre with a neutrophil component, protein 0.82 g/L and no oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Examination: Power 2 out of 5 in both legs, sensory level at T6, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, right relative afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity 6 out of 24 on the right
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid white cells 40 per microlitre, protein 0.82 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), glucose within normal limits, no oligoclonal bands, spinal magnetic resonance imaging shows a lesion spanning six vertebral segments

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Visual evoked potentials in both eyes to demonstrate subclinical optic pathway delay
Repeat magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with gadolinium in three months
Extractable nuclear antigen antibody panel including anti Ro and anti La antibodies
Commence interferon beta and arrange neurology follow up within the next month
Serum aquaporin four immunoglobulin G antibody assayed by a cell based method

subtopic_detail: the order of volume replacement and bone directed therapy in a drowsy dehydrated woman whose creatinine has risen with the calcium
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 68-year-old woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone who was brought in by her daughter. Over five days she has become increasingly drowsy, has vomited several times and has not opened her bowels.

Her daughter says she has been passing large volumes of urine and drinking very little, and that she slept most of yesterday. She takes no thiazide, no lithium and no calcium or vitamin D supplement, and she has had no recent imaging with contrast. Her creatinine three months ago was 78 micromol/L. She is rousable to voice and oriented to person only. Her mucous membranes are dry, her skin turgor is reduced and her jugular venous pressure is not visible with her lying flat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible supine, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.42 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90), urea 14.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50), parathyroid hormone less than 0.5 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent given at a brisk rate with close monitoring
Intravenous zoledronic acid at full dose given as a single infusion immediately
Intravenous furosemide given regularly to promote a calcium diuresis from the outset
Oral prednisolone at high dose with review of the calcium after forty eight hours
Urgent haemodialysis against a low calcium bath arranged through the renal unit

subtopic_detail: a widespread rash with facial swelling, fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis appearing five weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 62-year-old man who was started on allopurinol by his general practitioner five weeks ago after a third attack of gout. He has had four days of feeling hot and shivery and a rash that began on his trunk and has spread.

He says his face feels tight and his wife says his eyelids and cheeks look puffy. The rash is itchy rather than painful. He has not taken any other new medication, has had no recent travel and no unwell contacts. On examination there is a confluent red rash covering most of his trunk and limbs with facial swelling, and there are enlarged tender nodes in both sides of his neck and in his axillae. His lips, mouth, eyes and genitals are normal with no erosions, and the skin does not shear when firm lateral pressure is applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over more than half the body surface, periorbital and facial oedema, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), atypical lymphocytes present on film, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60 to 110), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and add a sedating antihistamine with topical corticosteroid
Cease allopurinol and commence systemic corticosteroid with staged organ monitoring
Cease allopurinol and arrange urgent transfer to the regional burns unit for care
Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous immunoglobulin over the next five days
Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous flucloxacillin for a presumed cellulitis

subtopic_detail: multiple vertebral fractures fourteen months after the last six monthly injection in a woman who simply stopped attending
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman who has had four days of severe pain between her shoulder blades that began as she lifted a box while unpacking after moving house.

She was treated with six monthly denosumab injections for five years for osteoporosis. She moved interstate fourteen months ago, did not transfer her care, and has had no injection since. She takes calcium and colecalciferol daily. She has had no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss. Radiographs today show new wedge compression fractures at the seventh and ninth thoracic vertebrae that were not present on a film taken two years ago. Her serum and urine protein electrophoresis, corrected calcium, thyroid function and myeloma screen are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Tender over the mid thoracic spinous processes, increased thoracic kyphosis, normal lower limb neurology, height 4 cm less than recorded five years ago
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone, creatinine and protein electrophoresis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her osteoporosis now?

options.text: Continue calcium and colecalciferol alone and repeat bone densitometry in two years
Withhold all antiresorptive treatment until the acute fractures have healed fully
Recommence denosumab now and plan a bisphosphonate before it is ever stopped again
Refer for percutaneous vertebroplasty of both fractured levels before any drug change
Commence teriparatide alone as she has fractured while on antiresorptive treatment

subtopic_detail: dusky coalescing macules with skin shearing and erosions at three mucosal sites three weeks after a rapidly titrated mood stabiliser
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar affective disorder and was titrated up quickly because of a transcription error on the prescription.

For two days she has had fever, a gritty burning sensation in both eyes and increasing pain in her mouth so that she cannot swallow her own saliva. Yesterday dusky flat spots appeared on her chest and have since joined together, and this morning the skin over her upper back and chest has begun to lift away in sheets. She describes the skin as burning and exquisitely painful rather than itchy. Gentle lateral pressure on apparently intact skin adjacent to a blister causes the epidermis to shear. Erosions are present on her lips, conjunctivae and vulva, and you estimate about twelve per cent of her body surface has detached.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 102/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dusky coalescing macules with flaccid blisters, epidermal detachment over about twelve per cent of body surface, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions of the lips, conjunctivae and vulva
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 4.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), urea 9.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start oral prednisolone with review in clinic in two days
Cease lamotrigine and apply potent topical corticosteroid with oral antihistamine
Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous flucloxacillin for staphylococcal skin disease
Cease lamotrigine and transfer urgently to a specialist burns or dermatology unit
Arrange a skin biopsy for frozen section before deciding on any transfer or treatment

subtopic_detail: recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, hyponatraemia and new proximal weakness after a sulfonamide antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to see a 27-year-old woman in the emergency department with four days of severe generalised abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. She has been unable to keep anything down and has eaten almost nothing.

This is her third presentation with the same pain in eighteen months. A diagnostic laparoscopy eight months ago was entirely normal and she was told the pain was functional. Five days ago her general practitioner started trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. She has also been following a strict low carbohydrate diet for three weeks. Today she cannot lift her arms above her head to tie her hair and her grip has weakened. She is agitated and tearful and keeps asking to go home. Her partner mentions that the urine in the bottle by her bed went a deep reddish brown after sitting on the windowsill overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness but no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, proximal upper limb power 3 out of 5 with reduced biceps and supinator reflexes, sensation intact, no rash and no basophilic stippling reported on film
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45 to 90), lipase and amylase within normal limits, haemoglobin 134 g/L (120 to 160), beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
Venous blood lead concentration with a blood film examined for basophilic stippling
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid protein and cell count to assess her weakness
Urine drug screen with paired serum and urine osmolality to explain the low sodium
Urinary porphobilinogen measured on a fresh sample protected from light exposure

subtopic_detail: deciding what must be excluded before iron is replaced in a middle aged man with microcytic anaemia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who has become breathless walking up the hill to his house over the past three months. He puts it down to getting older and having given up cycling.

He has no abdominal pain, has not noticed any blood in his stool and says his bowels are unchanged. He takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no anticoagulant. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has never had a gastroscopy or colonoscopy. He has not been invited to bowel screening because he moved address. His father had a colectomy in his sixties for a reason he was never told. His weight is stable and he has no night sweats. His examination shows conjunctival pallor with no abdominal mass, no organomegaly and a normal rectal examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 86/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no koilonychia, abdomen soft with no mass or organomegaly, rectal examination normal with brown stool
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-100), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16-45), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral iron and recheck the full blood count after three months of therapy
Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy while commencing iron replacement
Request a faecal occult blood test and investigate further only if it is positive
Perform haemoglobin electrophoresis before any endoscopic investigation is arranged
Arrange an intravenous iron infusion and review his symptoms again in six weeks

subtopic_detail: completing assessment of a discrete breast lump when the imaging report is reassuring but the clinical findings are not
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who found a lump in her left breast three weeks ago while showering. She has no breast pain and no nipple discharge.

She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and has never taken hormonal contraception. She had a screening mammogram eighteen months ago that was reported as normal. On examination there is a 2 cm firm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that does not move freely within the breast tissue, and there is mild tethering of the overlying skin when she raises her arm. There is no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Bilateral mammography and targeted ultrasound arranged by a colleague last week are both reported as showing no discrete abnormality in dense breast tissue.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm firm irregular mass in the left upper outer quadrant with reduced mobility and skin tethering on arm elevation, no nipple retraction or discharge, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: Bilateral mammography reports heterogeneously dense breast tissue with no discrete abnormality, targeted left breast ultrasound reports no discrete lesion identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for core biopsy of the palpable abnormality despite the imaging result
Reassure her that both imaging tests are normal and review her in three months
Repeat the mammogram with tomosynthesis views in a further six months' time
Arrange fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass in the practice this week
Check her serum tumour markers and refer only if the results are abnormal

subtopic_detail: separating an arrhythmic cause of collapse from a benign faint using the history and electrocardiogram
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who collapsed while playing indoor soccer an hour ago. His teammates say he dropped without warning, was briefly stiff with a few jerks, and was fully alert within thirty seconds.

He had no warmth, nausea, tunnel vision or sweating beforehand, and he does not remember falling. He has had two similar episodes in the past year, one while sprinting for a bus and one while swimming, both of which he attributed to dehydration. He has no tongue biting, no incontinence and no confusion afterwards. His father died suddenly at 41 while jogging and was never autopsied. He takes no medication and uses no drugs. He is currently asymptomatic with normal observations, and his examination reveals a systolic murmur that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg lying and 122/74 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, jerky carotid upstroke, no ankle oedema, chest clear, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads, electrolytes and troponin within normal limits, capillary glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with advice on hydration and salt intake for a vasovagal tendency
Arrange outpatient tilt table testing to confirm a neurally mediated mechanism
Load with an antiepileptic and refer to neurology for outpatient investigation
Admit for continuous cardiac monitoring with urgent inpatient echocardiography
Fit a 24 hour ambulatory monitor and review him in the clinic next week

subtopic_detail: managing a small solid pulmonary nodule found incidentally in a former smoker with no prior imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64-year-old woman after a computed tomography scan of the abdomen performed for suspected renal colic, which incidentally captured the lung bases and reported a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins.

She smoked fifteen cigarettes a day from age eighteen until she stopped nine years ago. She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and her exercise tolerance is unchanged. She has never had a chest radiograph or chest computed tomography before, so there is no earlier imaging for comparison. She has no history of malignancy and no known asbestos exposure. Her examination is normal with no lymphadenopathy, no clubbing and a clear chest. The radiologist notes no mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no pleural abnormality.

data_table.Examination: No clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation with equal expansion, no chest wall tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography reports a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy, no pleural effusion, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for computed tomography guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule
Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the metabolic activity
Refer for bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound and transbronchial sampling
Reassure her that a nodule of this size in a former smoker requires no follow up
Interval computed tomography surveillance determined by nodule diameter

subtopic_detail: preventing acute urate nephropathy before treating a bulky haematological malignancy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old man with a three week history of rapidly enlarging cervical and abdominal lymphadenopathy and night sweats. Biopsy has confirmed a high grade B cell lymphoma with a very high proliferation index, and chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow.

He has a large abdominal nodal mass and hepatosplenomegaly. He has no history of gout and takes no regular medication. He is of Southern European background and his glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase level has been requested but has not yet returned. He is passing urine normally. His lactate dehydrogenase is markedly raised, his urate is elevated, his potassium and phosphate are at the upper end of normal and his corrected calcium is at the lower end. His creatinine is mildly raised and his urine output has been adequate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bulky cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, abdominal mass palpable in the left upper quadrant, liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, no oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate dehydrogenase 1 840 U/L (120-250), urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), potassium 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 1.48 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before chemotherapy begins?

options.text: Oral allopurinol with encouragement to increase his oral fluid intake
Prophylactic haemodialysis via a temporary catheter before the first cycle
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine and improve urate clearance
Delay chemotherapy for one week and repeat the biochemistry before proceeding
Intravenous hydration with rasburicase once the enzyme result has returned

subtopic_detail: preventing viral reactivation before rituximab in a patient with resolved hepatitis B infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man newly diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma who is due to start rituximab based chemotherapy next week.

He was born in Vietnam and came to Australia at nineteen. He has never had jaundice and has never been told he has a liver problem. His pre treatment screening shows hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis B core antibody positive and hepatitis B surface antibody positive at a protective level, with hepatitis B viral load undetectable. His alanine aminotransferase is normal, his liver ultrasound is normal and his hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology are negative. The haematology team have asked whether anything is needed before the first cycle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, cervical lymphadenopathy consistent with his lymphoma
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody positive, surface antibody positive at a protective level, hepatitis B viral load undetectable, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 45), liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before starting his chemotherapy?

options.text: No specific action, since a negative surface antigen indicates cleared infection
Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster course before the first cycle of treatment
Commence antiviral prophylaxis before the immunosuppression begins
Monitor liver enzymes monthly and start an antiviral if the enzymes rise
Replace rituximab with a regimen that avoids B cell depleting monoclonal therapy

subtopic_detail: applying the diameter and growth thresholds for repair to an incidentally found aortic aneurysm in a fit older man
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 71-year-old man after an abdominal ultrasound arranged for intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, which showed gallstones and an incidental infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.8 cm in maximum anteroposterior diameter.

He has no back pain and no abdominal pain related to the aneurysm, and his abdomen is not tender. He smoked twenty cigarettes a day for forty years and stopped two years ago. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and his blood pressure today is 138/82 mmHg. He walks his dog for an hour daily without limitation and lives independently. He has no family history of aneurysm. A scan performed eleven months ago for renal colic reported the aorta as 4.6 cm, which no one had mentioned to him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with a pulsatile mass palpable above the umbilicus, femoral and pedal pulses present and equal, no abdominal bruit, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Current ultrasound 4.8 cm infrarenal aneurysm, ultrasound eleven months ago reported 4.6 cm, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for urgent vascular surgical repair within the next two weeks
Reassure him and repeat the ultrasound only if he develops abdominal symptoms
Arrange interval ultrasound surveillance with cardiovascular risk factor treatment
Start a beta blocker specifically to slow the rate of aneurysm expansion
Order computed tomography angiography now to plan endovascular stent grafting

subtopic_detail: investigating persistent symptoms twelve months after starting a gluten free diet for coeliac disease
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman diagnosed with coeliac disease twelve months ago on duodenal biopsy showing subtotal villous atrophy. She started a gluten free diet immediately after diagnosis.

She reports that her bloating and loose stools improved for about four months and have since returned, occurring most days. She has not lost weight, has no nocturnal diarrhoea, no rectal bleeding and no fever. She eats out two or three times a week and buys packaged foods, and she has not seen a dietitian since the month after her diagnosis. Her tissue transglutaminase antibody was 128 units at diagnosis, fell to 34 at six months and is 41 units today. Her haemoglobin and ferritin have normalised on oral iron and her albumin is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with mild distension, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no dermatitis herpetiformis, body mass index 24 kg/m2 and unchanged from diagnosis
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase antibody 128 units at diagnosis, 34 at six months and 41 today, haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist dietitian to review adherence and hidden exposure
Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory coeliac disease and reassess
Arrange computed tomography enterography to exclude small bowel lymphoma
Trial a low fermentable carbohydrate diet for coexisting irritable bowel syndrome
Repeat duodenal biopsy now to assess whether the villous architecture has recovered

subtopic_detail: lowering an extreme triglyceride concentration after an episode of pancreatitis with lipaemic serum
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man on day four of an admission with acute pancreatitis. His abdominal pain has settled and he has resumed a light oral diet.

The laboratory reported his admission serum as grossly lipaemic. His abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones and no biliary dilatation, and his admission alcohol history is twelve standard drinks most evenings for several years. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and has not attended review for two years. His admission triglycerides were 46 mmol/L and are 18 mmol/L today after fasting and insulin infusion. His amylase peaked at four times the upper limit of normal. He has eruptive xanthomas over both elbows and his father had pancreatitis in his forties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Crops of yellow papules over both elbows and knees, no tendon xanthomas, no corneal arcus, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, body mass index 33 kg/m2, hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Triglycerides 46 mmol/L on admission and 18 mmol/L today (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), haemoglobin A1c 82 mmol/mol (less than 53), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, lipase raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent a further episode?

options.text: Fenofibrate with alcohol abstinence, dietary fat restriction and glycaemic control
High intensity statin therapy titrated to a target low density lipoprotein level
Ezetimibe added to dietary modification with lipid review in three months
Regular therapeutic plasma exchange arranged as an ongoing outpatient program
Cholecystectomy on this admission to remove the likely source of the pancreatitis

subtopic_detail: separating drug induced prolactin elevation from a lactotroph adenoma when the level sits in an ambiguous range
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old woman whose periods stopped seven months ago. She has a negative pregnancy test and has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples.

She was started on risperidone 3 mg daily fourteen months ago for a psychotic illness and has been stable on it since, with no relapse and good adherence. She takes no other medication, no herbal preparations and no opioids. She has no headache and no visual symptoms. Her thyroid function is normal, her renal function is normal and she has no features of polycystic ovary syndrome. Her prolactin measured on two occasions without venepuncture stress is 2 400 mIU/L and then 2 550 mIU/L. Her formal visual field testing is normal and her body mass index is 23 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible galactorrhoea, no goitre, no hirsutism or acne, visual fields full on formal perimetry, no cranial nerve abnormality, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2 400 mIU/L and 2 550 mIU/L on two occasions (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45-90), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, oestradiol low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange pituitary magnetic resonance imaging and liaise with her psychiatrist
Stop the risperidone today and recheck the prolactin level in four weeks
Start cabergoline to restore her menstrual cycle and continue the risperidone
Reassure her that this is an expected drug effect and no further action is needed
Request macroprolactin screening on the stored sample before doing anything further

subtopic_detail: selecting which medicine to withdraw first in a frail older woman with recurrent falls and postural hypotension
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 84-year-old woman who has fallen three times in two months, most recently sustaining a skin tear to her forearm. She lives alone with daily assistance from her daughter.

She describes light headedness on standing from a chair and says the falls all happened shortly after she got up. Her medicines are perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night taken intermittently, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily and doxazosin 4 mg daily, which was started three months ago for nocturia. Her blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with reproduction of her symptoms. Her cognition is intact, her gait is steady when she is not light headed, her vitamin D is replete and her vision was checked this year.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with symptoms reproduced, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 14 seconds, no focal neurological deficit, no cerebellar signs, no peripheral neuropathy, heart sounds dual with no murmur, skin tear dressed on the left forearm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 76 nmol/L (50-150), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality, morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: Which medication would you withdraw first?

options.text: Atorvastatin, since its benefit at her age is limited and it may cause myalgia
Pantoprazole, since long term use is associated with fracture and infection risk
Amlodipine, since calcium channel blockade causes vasodilatation and ankle oedema
Doxazosin, since alpha blockade directly impairs the vasoconstrictor reflex on standing
Temazepam, since benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls in older adults

subtopic_detail: choosing therapy for amiodarone associated thyrotoxicosis when the gland shows absent vascularity
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar asked to see a 68-year-old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for fourteen months for recurrent ventricular tachycardia after an infarct. His implanted defibrillator has fired twice in the past fortnight.

Over three months he has lost 9 kg despite a good appetite, and he has a fine tremor and heat intolerance. He grew up in Adelaide and has no history of iodine deficiency or previous thyroid disease. There is no neck swelling and no eye signs. His thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine. His thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies are both negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows a normal sized gland with absent parenchymal vascularity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min irregular, blood pressure 138/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine resting tremor, warm moist palms, no goitre or thyroid bruit, no proptosis or lid retraction, no pretibial change, defibrillator generator palpable below the left clavicle
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 11.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies negative, colour flow Doppler shows absent parenchymal vascularity, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: High dose carbimazole alone titrated against repeat thyroid function testing
Oral corticosteroid for destructive thyroiditis with cardiology review of the amiodarone
Cease amiodarone and observe, since the thyrotoxicosis will settle once it clears
Radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid arranged as an outpatient procedure
Potassium perchlorate with lithium carbonate to block further iodide uptake

subtopic_detail: sequencing thiamine and glucose in a high anion gap acidosis where the blood sugar is not raised
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 49-year-old man brought in by ambulance with two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He drinks a bottle of spirits most days and has eaten almost nothing for three days since his last drink.

He is alert and oriented but looks unwell and dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. He has no focal abdominal tenderness, no guarding and no organomegaly. He has no history of diabetes and takes no medication. He has not taken any paracetamol, aspirin, antifreeze or methylated spirits, and his partner confirms there were no tablets or unusual containers at home. His venous gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap, his blood glucose is 4.1 mmol/L, his serum ketones are strongly positive, his lactate is mildly raised and his osmolar gap is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 114/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor, alert and oriented with Glasgow coma scale 15, no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, gait not tested, abdomen soft with generalised mild tenderness, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.24 with bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32) and anion gap 24 mmol/L, blood glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta hydroxybutyrate strongly positive, lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), osmolar gap normal, ethanol not detected, paracetamol and salicylate not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence an intravenous insulin infusion with hourly blood glucose monitoring
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis directly
Start fomepizole and arrange urgent haemodialysis for presumed toxic alcohol ingestion
Give oral carbohydrate and observe him for symptomatic improvement overnight
Intravenous thiamine followed by glucose containing fluid with volume replacement

subtopic_detail: the rebound that follows stopping a monoclonal antiresorptive without replacing it
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for three years after a wrist fracture. She tells you she has decided to stop because she dislikes injections and feels her bones must be stronger now. Her last injection was five months ago and the next is due in four weeks.

She has had no new fractures and no back pain. Her repeat bone density scan last month showed a lumbar spine T score improved from minus 2.9 to minus 2.2. Her renal function is normal, her corrected calcium is normal and her vitamin D is adequate on supplementation. She has no history of dental problems and no upper gastrointestinal symptoms, and she takes no corticosteroids.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No spinal tenderness, height unchanged from two years ago, no kyphosis, dentition in good condition
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), lumbar spine T score minus 2.2
data_table.Medications: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six monthly, colecalciferol 1000 units daily, calcium from diet

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Stop now and start teriparatide instead, given her improved bone density result
Start an oral bisphosphonate to begin when the next injection would have been due
Extend the dosing interval to twelve monthly as a compromise she may find acceptable
Continue the injections indefinitely because stopping is never appropriate with this drug
Agree to stop and repeat her bone density scan in two years to check for any loss

subtopic_detail: the fourth agent to add once three classes at maximum tolerated dose have not reached target
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58-year-old man whose blood pressure remains above target despite three medicines. His home readings over the past fortnight average 158/94 mmHg, and his clinic reading today is 162/96 mmHg in both arms.

He takes perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and indapamide 2.5 mg daily, all at maximum tolerated doses, and his dispensing history confirms he collects all three every month. He does not use non-steroidal anti inflammatories, decongestants or liquorice, drinks two standard drinks a week and does not snore or have witnessed apnoeas. His renal artery imaging last year was normal and his aldosterone to renin ratio was not suggestive of primary aldosteronism. His potassium today is 3.9 mmol/L and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 60.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 162/96 mmHg both arms, pulse rate 72/min regular, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29, no radiofemoral delay, no abdominal bruit, fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, aldosterone to renin ratio not elevated
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily

lead_in: Which medicine should you add next?

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg daily with electrolytes rechecked within one to two weeks
Candesartan 16 mg daily in addition to his current angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
Prazosin 1 mg twice daily, increasing the dose according to his tolerance
Bisoprolol 5 mg daily, titrating upward according to his heart rate response
Substitute hydrochlorothiazide for the indapamide before adding any further agent

subtopic_detail: committing an asymptomatic patient to lifelong replacement on the strength of a single abnormal result
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman who had thyroid function tested by an after hours service three weeks ago when she attended with a viral illness and fatigue. She feels completely well now and has come for the result.

Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 11.4 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 14 pmol/L. She has no cold intolerance, constipation, weight change, hair loss or menstrual change, and her energy has returned to normal since the illness settled. She is not pregnant, is not trying to conceive and uses an intrauterine device. She takes no amiodarone, lithium or iodine containing preparation and has had no neck surgery or radiation. Her pulse is 68 beats per minute and there is no goitre or nodule palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No goitre or palpable nodule, no periorbital puffiness, reflexes normal with normal relaxation phase, no dry skin
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 14 pmol/L (10-20), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start thyroxine 50 micrograms daily now and recheck the thyroid function in eight weeks
Arrange thyroid ultrasound to look for the structural cause of the abnormal result
Repeat the thyroid function tests in six to eight weeks with thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Reassure her that she is well and repeat the thyroid function only if symptoms appear
Measure free triiodothyronine now to establish whether her thyroid function is adequate

subtopic_detail: numb feet in a patient whose long standing medicine interferes with absorption of a vitamin
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has taken metformin 1 g twice daily for nine years. Over the past eight months he has noticed numbness and pins and needles in both feet, and more recently in his fingertips.

His most recent glycated haemoglobin was 6.8 per cent and has stayed below 7 per cent for six years. He drinks one beer on weekends and has no history of alcohol misuse. He has no back pain, no bladder symptoms and no weight loss. On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a mean cell volume of 103 fL with a normal haemoglobin, and his renal function, liver function and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration and proprioception to mid shin, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, Romberg positive, no pallor, tongue normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 103 fL (80-100), glycated haemoglobin 6.8 per cent, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone within range
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies to characterise the distribution of the neuropathy
Intensify glycaemic control, since neuropathy reflects inadequate long term diabetes management
Measure serum vitamin B12 with folate and consider methylmalonic acid if borderline
Check serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains for a paraproteinaemic cause
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to exclude a compressive cause

subtopic_detail: recurrent falls where the medication list rather than a new diagnosis explains the symptom
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 81-year-old man who has fallen four times in three months, twice in the bathroom on getting up at night and twice when standing from a chair after lunch. He has not been injured beyond bruising and has not lost consciousness.

He describes feeling lightheaded and greying out for a few seconds on standing, which resolves if he sits back down. There is no chest pain, palpitation or exertional symptom, and the episodes never happen while he is sitting or walking. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, indapamide, temazepam for sleep and oxybutynin for urinary urgency. His lying blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg falling to 108/62 mmHg after three minutes standing, with a pulse rate rising only from 68 to 74 beats per minute. His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Lying blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, standing blood pressure 108/62 mmHg at three minutes, pulse rate 68/min lying and 74/min standing, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal gait when observed unhurried, no cerebellar signs, proprioception intact, no cogwheel rigidity, timed up and go 14 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, haemoglobin 137 g/L (130-180), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), glucose within range
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor and an echocardiogram before changing any medicine
Start fludrocortisone to raise his standing blood pressure and continue the current regimen
Request computed tomography of the brain to exclude an intracranial cause for the falls
Reduce his antihypertensive burden and plan a staged withdrawal of the sedative and the anticholinergic
Refer for a falls prevention exercise program as the single intervention needed

subtopic_detail: an evening urge to move the legs where a routine blood test changes the treatment entirely
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 55-year-old woman with eighteen months of an uncomfortable crawling sensation in both legs that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse in bed. She has to get up and walk around, which relieves it completely until she lies down again.

She is losing about two hours of sleep most nights and is exhausted at work. The sensation is not painful and there is no burning or numbness. She has heavy periods that she has never had investigated. She takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antiemetics. Her neurological examination is normal with intact reflexes, power and sensation, and her peripheral pulses are present. Her full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 119 g/L with a mean cell volume of 78 fL, and her ferritin is 22 micrograms/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal power, tone, reflexes and sensation in both legs, pedal pulses present, no varicosities, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 78 fL (80-100), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid stimulating hormone within range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose taken two hours before her symptoms usually begin
Replace iron with the aim of raising the ferritin well above the lower limit of normal
Prescribe temazepam at night to restore her sleep while the symptoms are investigated
Arrange overnight polysomnography to document periodic limb movements during sleep
Start gabapentin at night, titrating the dose upward according to her symptom response

subtopic_detail: the size of creatinine rise after starting renin angiotensin blockade that should not stop the drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria who started ramipril 5 mg daily two weeks ago. She has come for the follow up blood test you arranged and feels entirely well.

Her creatinine has risen from 88 micromol/L before starting to 106 micromol/L today, and her potassium is 4.7 mmol/L. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, is drinking normally and has not started any anti inflammatory medicine. Her blood pressure today is 128/74 mmHg sitting, with no postural drop, and she has no oedema. Her urine albumin to creatinine ratio before starting was 42 mg/mmol. Her renal ultrasound last year showed normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/74 mmHg sitting with no postural drop, pulse rate 76/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no ankle oedema, no abdominal bruit, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 106 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 88, potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Halve the dose to 2.5 mg daily and recheck her renal function in four weeks
Stop the empagliflozin, since it is the more likely explanation for the creatinine rise
Arrange urgent renal artery imaging, since this degree of rise suggests arterial stenosis
Keep her on the current dose and confirm the result has plateaued on repeat testing
Stop the ramipril permanently and record it as having caused acute kidney injury

subtopic_detail: why a hypoglycaemic episode that has already corrected still requires admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 78-year-old woman brought in by ambulance after her daughter found her confused and sweating at home. The paramedics recorded a blood glucose of 1.8 mmol/L and gave intravenous glucose, after which she recovered completely within minutes.

Four hours later in the department she has become drowsy again with a blood glucose of 2.4 mmol/L, which responded to a further dose of glucose. She takes gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily and metformin, and her daughter says she has been eating poorly for three days because of a sore throat. She takes no insulin. Her creatinine is 142 micromol/L, risen from a baseline of 96. She lives alone and her daughter is returning interstate tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable during the second episode, alert between episodes, no focal neurology, mildly dry mucous membranes, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L during the second episode, creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 96, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glycated haemoglobin 6.4 per cent
data_table.Medications: Gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular glucagon and arrange review by her general practitioner tomorrow
Give a carbohydrate meal and discharge her once her glucose has been stable for two hours
Admit for a glucose infusion with regular monitoring and withhold the gliclazide
Halve the gliclazide dose and discharge her with instructions to monitor at home
Start octreotide now as the specific antidote and observe her in the short stay unit

subtopic_detail: maintaining time critical dopaminergic dosing in a patient who cannot take anything by mouth
stem:
You are the surgical resident admitting a 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease of eleven years duration who has a small bowel obstruction and is being kept nil by mouth pending theatre tomorrow. A nasogastric tube is in place on free drainage.

He takes levodopa with carbidopa at 6 am, 10 am, 2 pm, 6 pm and 10 pm, and he tells you his movement becomes very difficult within an hour of a late dose. The intern has charted his usual doses as three times daily with meals and has added metoclopramide for nausea. It is now 9 am and his 6 am dose was not given because he was in the emergency department. He is currently rigid, barely able to turn in bed and speaking softly, and he was walking independently at home yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked rigidity with bradykinesia, soft hypophonic speech, unable to turn unaided in bed, abdomen distended with tinkling bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), abdominal computed tomography showing small bowel obstruction with a transition point
data_table.Medications: Levodopa with carbidopa five times daily, metoclopramide charted as required, nil by mouth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold all his medicines until after theatre and restart them when he is eating again
Convert him to a rotigotine patch at an equivalent dose and leave the metoclopramide charted
Accept the three times daily charting as close enough and give the doses with the drug round
Give intravenous apomorphine as a bolus now and reassess his rigidity in thirty minutes
Give the levodopa through the nasogastric tube at his exact home times and cease the metoclopramide

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic choice for moderate community acquired pneumonia in a man with a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin
stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to your emergency department with four days of fever, productive cough and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He is admitted under your medical team.

His medical record documents an episode ten years ago in which amoxicillin caused urticaria, lip swelling and hypotension requiring adrenaline in an emergency department. He has no other allergies. On examination he has bronchial breathing at the right base with dullness to percussion. His chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. His severity assessment places him in the moderate category requiring inpatient intravenous therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion at the right base, no signs of effusion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 186 mg/L (<5), urea 7.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
Intravenous vancomycin with oral azithromycin and review when culture results return
Intravenous moxifloxacin as a single agent with review when culture results return
Oral doxycycline as a single agent with review when culture results return and reassessment daily

subtopic_detail: Management of an international normalised ratio of six point five on warfarin with no bleeding before elective surgery
stem:
A 74-year-old woman taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation attends your anticoagulation clinic for a routine check three weeks before an elective hip replacement. Her target range is 2.0 to 3.0 and her results have been stable for months.

She completed a course of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection last week. She reports no bruising, no bleeding from the gums or nose, no blood in the urine or stool and no headache. Her examination reveals no bruising or other signs of bleeding. Her international normalised ratio today is 6.5 and her haemoglobin is unchanged from her last check.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No bruising, petechiae or other signs of bleeding, no abdominal tenderness, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.5 (target 2.0-3.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold warfarin alone and repeat the measurement in two days without giving vitamin K
Withhold warfarin and give low dose oral vitamin K, with a repeat measurement the next day
Withhold warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg, with a repeat measurement the next day
Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate, with a repeat measurement the next day
Continue warfarin at a reduced dose and repeat the measurement in one week without other action

subtopic_detail: Muscle aching without weakness and a normal creatine kinase six weeks after starting a statin
stem:
A 58-year-old man attends your practice six weeks after starting atorvastatin 40 mg daily for secondary prevention following a myocardial infarction. He reports aching in both thighs and shoulders that came on gradually over the past fortnight.

He describes it as a dull ache rather than weakness, and he can still climb stairs and rise from a chair without difficulty. His urine is a normal colour. On examination his power is 5 out of 5 in all muscle groups with no tenderness and normal reflexes. His creatine kinase, thyroid function, renal function and liver enzymes are all within normal limits. He tells you he has read that statins damage muscle and he wants to stop the drug permanently.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Power 5 out of 5 in all muscle groups, no muscle tenderness, normal reflexes, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 142 U/L (<200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits, liver enzymes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the statin permanently and manage his lipids with dietary measures and exercise alone
Continue the same statin at the same dose and add coenzyme Q10 supplementation daily
Continue the same statin and arrange electromyography with a muscle biopsy for further assessment
Cease the statin permanently and commence a proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin inhibitor now
Cease the statin for a washout period, then rechallenge at a lower dose of a different statin

subtopic_detail: Neurological symptoms with a normal serum cobalamin and a raised methylmalonic acid in a man on long term metformin
stem:
A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends your practice with six months of pins and needles in both feet that has progressed to his lower calves, and increasing unsteadiness when walking in the dark.

He has taken metformin 2 g daily for eleven years and his glycated haemoglobin has been consistently at target. On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a normal haemoglobin with a mean cell volume at the upper end of the range. His serum cobalamin is 165 pmol/L, his methylmalonic acid is raised and his homocysteine is raised. His thyroid function and folate are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense to mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes, positive Romberg test, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 99 fL (80-100), serum cobalamin 165 pmol/L (150-700), methylmalonic acid raised, homocysteine raised, folate and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that the serum level is within range and review his symptoms again in six months
Attribute the symptoms to diabetic neuropathy and commence duloxetine for symptomatic relief
Start parenteral cobalamin replacement now without waiting for further confirmatory testing
Start oral folic acid replacement now and recheck his metabolites and blood count in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine before starting any replacement therapy

subtopic_detail: Acidosis with ketones and a glucose of nine on day two after surgery in a man taking a sodium glucose cotransporter inhibitor
stem:
You are called to review a 54-year-old man on the surgical ward on day two after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He has become nauseated with abdominal discomfort and is breathing deeply, and the nursing staff are concerned he looks unwell.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and empagliflozin, both of which were charted and given on the morning of surgery. He has been eating very little since the operation. His abdomen is soft with mild port site tenderness only, and his surgical wounds look clean. His blood glucose measured on the ward is 9.2 mmol/L, which the intern notes is close to his usual reading.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Deep sighing respiration, soft abdomen with mild port site tenderness, clean wounds, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 9.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.19 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32), beta hydroxybutyrate 4.8 mmol/L (<0.6), anion gap 22 mmol/L (8-16), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (<2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride alone with hourly glucose monitoring and no insulin given
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis with hourly blood gas monitoring
Urgent computed tomography of the abdomen to exclude a surgical cause for the acidosis
Intravenous insulin infusion with concurrent glucose and fluid replacement, ceasing the empagliflozin
Subcutaneous rapid acting insulin given as required with four hourly glucose monitoring

subtopic_detail: Fragmented red cells with a platelet count of eleven and normal coagulation studies in a woman with confusion
stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with four days of increasing tiredness, bruising and intermittent confusion that her partner describes as her losing the thread mid-sentence. She has had no bleeding and no recent diarrhoea.

She takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection. On examination she is pale with scattered bruises over her limbs and scleral icterus, and she is oriented to person and place but not time. She is afebrile with no neck stiffness and no focal neurological deficit. Her blood film is reported as showing numerous fragmented red cells with marked thrombocytopenia. Her renal function is mildly impaired.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale with scattered limb bruising and scleral icterus, oriented to person and place but not time, no neck stiffness, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-155), platelets 11 x10^9/L (150-400), lactate dehydrogenase 1180 U/L (120-250), bilirubin 46 micromol/L (<20), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.3), fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (2.0-4.0), direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfuse platelets urgently to reduce bleeding risk and arrange plasma exchange afterwards
Arrange urgent plasma exchange and withhold platelet transfusion despite the low count
Give fresh frozen plasma with cryoprecipitate to correct the consumptive coagulopathy present
Start high dose oral corticosteroid alone and review her blood count again in forty eight hours
Commence broad spectrum antibiotics and arrange lumbar puncture to investigate the confusion

subtopic_detail: Reperfusion choice for obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism in a woman five days after intracranial surgery
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the neurosurgical ward to review a 61-year-old woman five days after craniotomy for resection of a meningioma. She has become acutely breathless and is now hypotensive despite a litre of crystalloid.

She was started on prophylactic enoxaparin yesterday. She is alert but distressed, with cool peripheries and a raised jugular venous pressure. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her calves are soft and non-tender. A bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle with septal flattening and a small underfilled left ventricle. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography confirms bilateral central filling defects. Her most recent computed tomography head scan yesterday showed expected postoperative changes with a small volume of blood in the resection cavity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg after one litre of crystalloid, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 89% on 15 L/min via reservoir mask, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert but distressed, cool peripheries, raised jugular venous pressure, chest clear on auscultation, calves soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 180 ng/L (<14), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (<2.0), echocardiogram shows dilated right ventricle with septal flattening, computed tomography pulmonary angiography shows bilateral central filling defects, head scan yesterday shows a small volume of blood in the resection cavity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase, since the haemodynamic compromise outweighs the bleeding risk
Therapeutic anticoagulation alone with a heparin infusion and close haemodynamic monitoring
Catheter directed or surgical clot removal, with systemic thrombolysis withheld given the recent surgery
Insertion of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter with no other reperfusion measure undertaken
Further large volume crystalloid resuscitation with vasopressor support and no reperfusion measure

subtopic_detail: Jaundice with a mixed liver enzyme pattern six weeks after starting long term urinary prophylaxis
stem:
A 67-year-old woman attends your practice with three weeks of fatigue, nausea and itching, and her daughter has noticed that her eyes look yellow. Six weeks ago she was started on long term nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for recurrent urinary infections.

She drinks no alcohol and takes no other prescribed medication, herbal preparations or supplements. She has had no abdominal pain, no fever and no rash. Her viral hepatitis serology is negative and her liver ultrasound shows a normal biliary tree with no dilatation and no focal lesion. Her antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1 in 160 and her immunoglobulin G is mildly raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 640 U/L (<35), alkaline phosphatase 290 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 78 micromol/L (<20), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.3), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), viral hepatitis serology negative, antinuclear antibody 1 in 160, immunoglobulin G mildly raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the drug and monitor with serial liver enzymes before considering immunosuppression
Continue the drug and commence corticosteroid therapy for presumed autoimmune hepatitis
Cease the drug and commence corticosteroid therapy immediately without a period of observation
Cease the drug and arrange urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography for the cholestasis
Continue the drug and arrange a liver biopsy to establish the histological diagnosis first

subtopic_detail: Advice for a woman on long term corticosteroid replacement who develops vomiting and diarrhoea while travelling
stem:
A 44-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency telephones your practice from a coastal town where she is on holiday. She takes hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon, together with fludrocortisone.

She has had watery diarrhoea and two episodes of vomiting since this morning after a restaurant meal, and several others in her group are similarly unwell. She feels weak and lightheaded but is alert and able to speak in full sentences, and she has managed to keep down some sips of water. She has her emergency injection kit with her and has used it once before. She asks what she should do.

data_table.Symptoms: Watery diarrhoea and two episodes of vomiting since this morning, weakness and lightheadedness, alert and speaking in full sentences
data_table.Medication: Hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon with fludrocortisone, emergency injection kit available
data_table.Context: Several members of her travelling group similarly unwell after a shared meal

lead_in: What advice would you give?

options.text: Continue her usual hydrocortisone dose and increase her fluid intake with oral rehydration solution
Double the usual fludrocortisone dose and keep the hydrocortisone dose unchanged for now
Use the emergency intramuscular injection immediately and then attend the nearest emergency department
Withhold the fludrocortisone until the diarrhoea settles and keep the hydrocortisone dose unchanged
Double the usual oral hydrocortisone and use the injection if vomiting prevents her keeping it down

subtopic_detail: Decision to continue resuscitation in a cardiac arrest after prolonged immersion with a core temperature of twenty six degrees
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a regional emergency department when a 24-year-old man is brought in after being pulled from a mountain river. He was in the water for an estimated forty minutes before being recovered.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started at the scene and has continued throughout a thirty minute transport. He is in cardiac arrest with a rhythm of ventricular fibrillation that has not responded to three shocks. His pupils are fixed and dilated and he is rigid, with no spontaneous respiratory effort. His oesophageal temperature reads 26 °C. There is no evidence of major trauma and no lethal injury is apparent.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation refractory to three shocks, oesophageal temperature 26 °C, no spontaneous respiratory effort
data_table.Examination: Fixed dilated pupils, generalised rigidity, no evidence of major trauma, no obviously lethal injury
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous pH 7.18 (7.32-7.42), glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Continue resuscitation with active rewarming before any decision to stop is considered
Cease resuscitation now, given the fixed dilated pupils and the rigidity on examination
Continue resuscitation with repeated shocks and adrenaline at the standard interval throughout
Cease resuscitation now, given the failure of three shocks to restore a perfusing rhythm
Continue resuscitation with passive external rewarming alone using blankets and a warm environment

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a reduced ratio on spirometry performed without a bronchodilator in a lifelong smoker
stem:
A 58-year-old woman attends your practice with three years of breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough. She has smoked fifteen cigarettes daily since her twenties.

She has had two chest infections in the past year, each treated with antibiotics. She reports that her breathlessness varies considerably, being worse on some days than others, and that she wakes occasionally at night with chest tightness. Her practice nurse performed spirometry this morning without administering a bronchodilator first. Her chest radiograph shows no focal abnormality and no hyperinflation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Scattered expiratory wheeze, no crackles, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in one second 1.72 L at 64 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 2.80 L, ratio 0.61, no bronchodilator given, chest radiograph unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and commence a long-acting bronchodilator now
Diagnose asthma and commence an inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting bronchodilator now
Repeat the spirometry after a bronchodilator to establish whether the obstruction persists
Arrange computed tomography of the chest to assess for emphysema before any treatment is started
Measure the transfer factor for carbon monoxide before making any diagnosis or starting treatment

subtopic_detail: Dosing decision for a glycopeptide antibiotic on day four when the creatinine has risen and the next dose is due
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 73-year-old man on day four of intravenous vancomycin for a methicillin resistant staphylococcal bacteraemia arising from an infected dialysis catheter that has since been removed.

He has improved clinically, is afebrile and his repeat blood cultures are negative. He also received two days of gentamicin on admission before the organism was identified.
