His creatinine was 88 micromol/L on admission and is 176 micromol/L today, with a urine output of 0.6 mL/kg/h over the past twelve hours. His next vancomycin dose is due in one hour and the nursing staff ask whether to give it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Catheter exit site clean after removal, no new murmur, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 176 micromol/L rising from 88 on admission, urine output 0.6 mL/kg/h over twelve hours, repeat blood cultures negative, last vancomycin level not yet taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action regarding the next dose?

options.text: Give the dose as charted and measure a level before the dose that follows it tomorrow
Give half the charted dose now and continue at that reduced dose without measuring a level
Cease the vancomycin entirely and switch to oral antibiotic therapy to complete the course
Withhold the dose and measure a level now, redosing according to the result and renal function
Give the dose as charted and commence intravenous fluid to protect renal function overnight

subtopic_detail: Sequencing of blockade before adrenalectomy when a beta blocker has already been started
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman referred with episodes of pounding headache, drenching sweats and a racing heart that come on without warning, last about twenty minutes and leave her exhausted.

Her blood pressure has been persistently high at clinic and at home. The results of the tests arranged by her general practitioner have returned, along with imaging. On reviewing the medication chart you see that the admitting intern started metoprolol yesterday evening for the tachycardia, and since then her blood pressure readings have been higher rather than lower. The surgical team has been consulted about adrenalectomy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 186/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines markedly elevated at more than four times the upper reference limit, potassium and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass with high unenhanced attenuation
data_table.Current medication: Metoprolol started yesterday evening, no other antihypertensive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her management?

options.text: Continue the beta blocker alone and refer for surgery in two weeks
Add a calcium channel blocker to the beta blocker and refer for surgery
Stop all antihypertensives until the day of the planned operation
Cease the beta blocker and start alpha blockade before any beta blockade
Add an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor to the beta blocker

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis threshold at the time of starting antiretroviral therapy
stem:
You are the registrar in an infectious diseases clinic seeing a 36-year-old man diagnosed with HIV three weeks ago after presenting with oral thrush and six months of intermittent night sweats.

He feels reasonably well and has no cough, breathlessness, headache or visual symptoms. His chest radiograph is clear and his examination is unremarkable apart from the treated oral candidiasis. His baseline bloods are back and antiretroviral therapy is being started today. He has no drug allergies, and his glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Immune status: CD4 count 140 cells/microlitre, HIV viral load 180000 copies/mL
data_table.Other results: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits, chest radiograph clear, toxoplasma and cryptococcal antigen negative
data_table.Allergies: No known drug allergies, normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity

lead_in: Which additional treatment should be started alongside his antiretroviral therapy?

options.text: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole as prophylaxis against pneumocystis
Weekly azithromycin as prophylaxis against mycobacterial infection
No prophylaxis until the CD4 count falls below fifty cells per microlitre
Fluconazole as continuing prophylaxis against recurrent fungal disease
No prophylaxis at all because antiretroviral therapy is being started

subtopic_detail: Adjunct that reduces recurrence in a first episode of acute pericarditis
stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department where you are the registrar, with two days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and eases when he sits forward. He had a viral upper respiratory illness a fortnight ago.

He is haemodynamically stable and comfortable sitting up. On auscultation you hear a scratchy sound over the left sternal edge that varies with his position. His troponin taken on arrival and repeated at three hours are both within normal limits, and a bedside echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function with no pericardial collection. He has been started on regular ibuprofen with good effect. He takes no regular medication and his renal function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Scratchy friction rub at the left sternal edge varying with position, no pulsus paradoxus, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Widespread concave upward ST elevation with PR segment depression, reciprocal changes in aVR
data_table.Investigations: Serial troponin within normal limits, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), echocardiogram shows normal function with no effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.text: Add prednisolone at moderate dose and taper it over four weeks
Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue the anti inflammatory alone
Start therapeutic anticoagulation and admit for cardiac monitoring
Arrange urgent coronary angiography before any further treatment
Add colchicine to the anti inflammatory and continue for three months

subtopic_detail: Transfusion strategy for acute chest syndrome with hypoxia during a vaso-occlusive admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward to review a 24-year-old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease who was admitted three days ago with severe limb and back pain and is receiving opioid analgesia.

Overnight she developed a fever and pleuritic chest pain, and this morning she is breathless at rest and needing increasing oxygen. Her chest radiograph, which was clear on admission, now shows new consolidation involving two lobes. Her haemoglobin has fallen from her documented baseline and her reticulocyte count is high. Intravenous antibiotics have been commenced and the haematology consultant is on her way in.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 62 g/L (115-155), baseline documented at 88 g/L, platelets 148 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes elevated
data_table.Imaging: New consolidation involving two lobes on chest radiograph, clear on admission
data_table.Treatment so far: Intravenous antibiotics commenced, opioid analgesia continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate transfusion strategy?

options.text: Simple top up transfusion of two units with continued oxygen therapy
Intravenous fluids at twice maintenance with continued opioid analgesia
Urgent exchange transfusion with respiratory support and antibiotics
Hydroxycarbamide started immediately with continued supportive care
Therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed pulmonary thromboembolism

subtopic_detail: Treatment of raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema and normal neuroimaging
stem:
A 28-year-old woman is referred to your general medical clinic with four months of daily headache that is worst when she first wakes and when she bends forward. She has also noticed brief greying of vision in both eyes when she stands up quickly, lasting a few seconds each time.

She describes a whooshing sound in both ears in time with her pulse. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she has gained 14 kg over two years. She takes no medication other than the combined oral contraceptive pill and has never taken tetracyclines or vitamin A derivatives. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs with blurred margins. Formal visual field testing shows an enlarged blind spot on both sides with otherwise preserved fields.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit, no meningism, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and magnetic resonance venography both reported as normal with no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis
data_table.Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 cmH2O, cerebrospinal fluid cell count, protein and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures as the mainstay of treatment
Acetazolamide with weight management and visual field monitoring
Referral for urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration this admission
Prednisolone at high dose with a slow taper over three months
Topiramate alone with review of the headache in three months

subtopic_detail: Opioid rotation when morphine metabolites accumulate as renal function declines
stem:
You are the registrar on the palliative care ward looking after a 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful bone disease. He has been comfortable for six weeks on sustained release oral morphine with occasional immediate release doses.

Over the past three days his family have noticed he is drowsy through the day, and twice they have seen sudden brief jerks of his arms while he dozes. Overnight he became restless and was briefly confused about where he was. His pain is no worse than before. His creatinine has risen progressively over the past fortnight and his urine output has fallen. His calcium is within normal limits, he is not hypoxic and his blood glucose is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, intermittent multifocal myoclonic jerks, pupils 2 mm bilaterally, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Biochemistry: Creatinine 268 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 18 mL/min/1.73m2, corrected calcium and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Sustained release oral morphine with immediate release breakthrough doses, unchanged for six weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his analgesia?

options.text: Increase the morphine dose to control the increasing agitation
Add midazolam and continue the morphine at the current dose
Add haloperidol for the agitation and continue the morphine unchanged
Stop the morphine and rotate to fentanyl or hydromorphone
Continue morphine but give it by subcutaneous infusion instead

subtopic_detail: Classifying a pleural effusion when the absolute protein and the protein ratio disagree
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 55-year-old man who has had three weeks of breathlessness on exertion and a dull ache in the right chest. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily for thirty years and has lost 5 kg.

He has no orthopnoea or ankle swelling, his jugular venous pressure is not elevated and his echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function. He takes no diuretics and has never taken any. His liver function and albumin are within normal limits and there is no ascites. A diagnostic pleural tap has been performed and the fluid and paired serum results are now available. The resident tells you the fluid must be a transudate because the protein is under 30 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note and reduced breath sounds at the right base, no peripheral oedema, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 28 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 210 U/L, straw coloured, cytology pending
data_table.Paired serum: Protein 46 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 295 U/L with a laboratory upper reference limit of 250 U/L, albumin within normal limits

lead_in: How should the fluid be classified and why?

options.text: An exudate, because the protein and lactate dehydrogenase ratios are raised
A transudate, because the pleural fluid protein is below 30 g/L
A transudate, so he should be treated with diuretics and observation
Indeterminate, so the tap should be repeated in one week to classify it
Indeterminate, so the fluid glucose and pH should be used to classify it

subtopic_detail: Sequencing joint aspiration and antibiotics in a monoarthritis in an immunosuppressed patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 62-year-old woman with a two day history of a hot, swollen and exquisitely painful right knee that she cannot bear weight on.

She has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and takes weekly methotrexate and low dose prednisolone. Her other joints are at their usual baseline and none is acutely inflamed. She is febrile and her inflammatory markers are markedly raised. She is haemodynamically stable with no hypotension or features of shock. The resident has drawn up intravenous flucloxacillin and is about to administer it while the orthopaedic registrar is being contacted about aspiration.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Right knee hot, swollen and tense with a large effusion, all movement severely restricted by pain, other joints at baseline
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5), urate within normal limits, blood cultures taken
data_table.Medication: Weekly methotrexate and low dose prednisolone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give the intravenous flucloxacillin now and aspirate the knee tomorrow
Start oral prednisolone for a presumed inflammatory arthritis flare
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee before any aspiration
Start colchicine for a presumed crystal arthropathy and review later
Aspirate the joint for urgent culture before antibiotics are given

subtopic_detail: Order of agents when controlling blood pressure in acute aortic dissection
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to the emergency department to see a 58-year-old man who developed severe tearing pain between his shoulder blades while getting out of his car two hours ago. The pain was maximal at onset.

He has long standing hypertension and has not taken his medication for several weeks. He is alert and in obvious distress. Peripheral pulses are present and symmetrical and there is no aortic regurgitant murmur or neurological deficit. His computed tomography aortogram has just been reported. On arriving you find that a glyceryl trinitrate infusion was started ten minutes ago and is being titrated upwards, and his heart rate has risen since it began.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 194/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical peripheral pulses, no diastolic murmur, no focal neurological deficit, chest clear
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography aortogram shows an intimal flap arising distal to the left subclavian artery extending to the level of the diaphragm, with no branch vessel compromise
data_table.Current treatment: Glyceryl trinitrate infusion commenced ten minutes ago and being titrated upwards, morphine given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate change to his management?

options.text: Continue the nitrate infusion alone and titrate it to the blood pressure
Start intravenous beta blockade before continuing the vasodilator
Start a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker as the single agent
Give intravenous hydralazine boluses to bring the pressure down fast
Withhold all antihypertensives until surgical review has been completed

subtopic_detail: Recognising respiratory failure in myasthenia gravis when oxygen saturation remains normal
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, maintained on pyridostigmine and azathioprine, who was admitted yesterday with a chest infection. She was started on a macrolide antibiotic by the admitting team.

Since this morning her voice has become nasal, she is struggling to swallow her tablets, and she describes her breathing as feeling like hard work although she does not feel short of breath lying still. She is anxious and using her accessory muscles intermittently. The nursing staff report that her oxygen saturation has remained normal throughout. Serial bedside spirometry performed by the physiotherapist shows her forced vital capacity has fallen from 1.9 L on admission to 1.4 L this morning and 0.9 L twenty minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Nasal speech, weak cough, bilateral ptosis, poor palatal elevation, intermittent accessory muscle use, chest clear to auscultation
data_table.Serial vital capacity: 1.9 L on admission, 1.4 L this morning, 0.9 L twenty minutes ago
data_table.Medication: Pyridostigmine and azathioprine maintained, macrolide antibiotic commenced yesterday

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose and observe on the ward overnight
Give high flow oxygen and repeat the vital capacity in the morning
Start high dose prednisolone alone and continue the antibiotic course
Arrange ventilatory support and plasma exchange, ceasing the antibiotic
Administer intravenous edrophonium to distinguish the type of crisis

subtopic_detail: Order of drug administration in decompensated thyrotoxicosis precipitated by infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 44-year-old woman brought in by her partner because she has become confused and agitated over the past day.

She was diagnosed with Graves disease eight months ago but stopped attending appointments and has not taken her tablets for several months. She has had a productive cough for five days. On examination she is agitated and disoriented, with warm sweaty skin, a fine tremor and a smooth goitre with a bruit. Her heart is irregularly irregular at a rapid rate and she has bibasal crackles. Her thyroid function has been sent urgently and cultures have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 106/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 39.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and disoriented, smooth goitre with a bruit, fine tremor, warm peripheries, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, liver function mildly deranged, thyroid function pending
data_table.Other: Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation, blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Give iodine first to block release then add a thionamide afterwards
Give a beta blocker and a thionamide before any iodine is administered
Give intravenous levothyroxine with supportive care and active cooling
Start amiodarone for rate control of the atrial fibrillation
Arrange urgent thyroidectomy before starting any medical therapy

subtopic_detail: Asymmetric oligoarthritis with nail pitting and a scaly rash
stem:
A 42-year-old plumber attends your general practice with four months of pain and swelling in his right knee, left ankle and the whole of his left fourth toe, which he says looks like a sausage.

He has morning stiffness lasting about an hour that eases as the day goes on. He has had scaly patches behind his ears and at his hairline for years which he treats with a shampoo from the chemist. His fingernails have small dents in them and one is lifting away from the nail bed. Rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are both negative, and urate is normal. Plain radiographs of the hands show no erosion.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Swollen right knee with effusion, swollen left ankle, diffuse swelling of the entire left fourth toe, nail pitting with onycholysis, scaly plaques at the hairline and retroauricular area
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), hand radiographs show no erosion
data_table.Symptom pattern: Morning stiffness of one hour improving with activity, asymmetric joint involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start colchicine and arrange joint aspiration for crystal analysis
Start a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug and review in a year
Reassure him that seronegative tests exclude an inflammatory cause
Start methotrexate and refer him to a rheumatology service
Refer him to dermatology for management of the psoriatic skin disease

subtopic_detail: Raised transferrin saturation with fatigue and arthralgia in a middle aged man
stem:
A 46-year-old man of northern European ancestry attends your general practice with a year of tiredness and aching in the second and third knuckles of both hands. He drinks about six standard drinks a week.

He has no known liver disease and takes no supplements, including no iron tablets. His brother was told at the age of fifty that he had too much iron and now has regular venesection. Examination shows no hepatomegaly, no spider naevi and no skin pigmentation. His fasting transferrin saturation is 68 percent on two separate occasions and his ferritin is 940 micrograms per litre. His C reactive protein is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, no hepatomegaly, no spider naevi, no skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Fasting transferrin saturation 68 percent (less than 45), ferritin 940 micrograms per litre (30-300), alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L (less than 45), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L
data_table.Family history: Brother diagnosed with iron overload at fifty and on venesection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request a liver biopsy
Repeat his ferritin level
Arrange hepatitis serology
Advise alcohol cessation
Request HFE genotyping

subtopic_detail: Episodic flushing with diarrhoea and a right sided cardiac murmur
stem:
A 58-year-old woman attends your clinic with two years of episodes in which her face and upper chest become hot and deep red for several minutes, sometimes several times a week. They are not associated with sweating and often follow a glass of wine or a cheese board.

She also has loose stools four to six times daily that have been attributed to irritable bowel syndrome, and she has lost 5 kg. She has not had night sweats. She is not menopausal, having had regular periods until last year, and a trial of an oestrogen preparation made no difference to the episodes. On auscultation there is a systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases on inspiration, and her jugular venous pressure shows prominent v waves.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, prominent jugular venous v waves, hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, telangiectasia over the cheeks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, thyroid function and coeliac serology all within normal limits, C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin within normal limits
data_table.Symptom pattern: Dry flushing lasting minutes, often triggered by alcohol and aged cheese, with chronic loose stools and weight loss

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure urinary five hydroxyindoleacetic acid
Measure plasma free metanephrine levels
Measure serum follicle stimulating hormone
Measure serum tryptase during an episode
Measure serum vasoactive intestinal peptide

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal leg restlessness with a ferritin in the low normal range
stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends your general practice with eighteen months of an unpleasant crawling sensation deep in both calves that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse when she goes to bed.

She describes an overwhelming need to move her legs, and says that walking around the house relieves it completely while she is moving. Her partner reports that she kicks in her sleep. She is exhausted during the day. She has no numbness, no weakness and no back pain, and her ankle reflexes and pedal pulses are normal. Her renal function and thyroid function are normal and she is not pregnant. She takes no antidepressant, antihistamine or antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal power, normal sensation to light touch and pinprick, ankle reflexes present, pedal pulses palpable, no varicosities
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 30 micrograms per litre (30-300), transferrin saturation 18 percent, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Symptom pattern: Onset at rest in the evening, relieved completely by movement, worse at night, partner reports periodic limb movements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start oral iron replacement and recheck her iron studies
Start pregabalin at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
Start a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the sleep disturbance
Refer for nerve conduction studies before any treatment is started

subtopic_detail: Cholestatic liver enzymes with a positive antimitochondrial antibody
stem:
A 54-year-old woman attends your general practice with nine months of tiredness and itching that is worst at night and affects her whole body. She scratches until she bleeds and has not slept properly for months.

She drinks two standard drinks a week and takes no regular medication, herbal preparation or supplement. She has no jaundice, no abdominal pain and no pale stools or dark urine. Her alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase are raised with only a mild rise in transaminases. An abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture with no biliary dilatation and no gallstones. Antimitochondrial antibody is positive at a high titre and her immunoglobulin M is raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations, no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no xanthelasma, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L (30-110), gamma glutamyl transferase 310 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), antimitochondrial antibody positive at high titre, immunoglobulin M raised, viral hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound shows normal liver texture, no biliary dilatation, no gallstones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start prednisolone and azathioprine and monitor her biochemistry
Refer for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography urgently
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and monitor her liver biochemistry
Start colestyramine alone and review her symptoms in three months
Arrange a liver biopsy before committing her to any drug treatment

subtopic_detail: Muscle aches with a moderately raised creatine kinase on a statin
stem:
A 61-year-old man attends your general practice with six weeks of aching and heaviness in both thighs and shoulders that makes getting out of a low chair harder than it used to be. He started atorvastatin 40 mg daily four months ago after a myocardial infarction.

He has not changed his exercise, has done no unaccustomed heavy work and has not started any new medication, including no antifungal, macrolide or fibrate. He drinks minimal alcohol. His urine is normal in colour and his renal function is unchanged from baseline. He is worried because he has been told he must never stop the tablet after a heart attack.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexors and shoulder abductors, no rash, no muscle tenderness, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 840 U/L (less than 200), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110) unchanged from baseline, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urinalysis negative for blood
data_table.Medication: Atorvastatin 40 mg daily for four months, aspirin, metoprolol, perindopril, no new interacting drug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the statin dose and recheck his creatine kinase in two weeks
Continue the statin unchanged and review his symptoms in three months
Stop the statin permanently and record a statin allergy in his file
Withhold the statin and check his thyroid function before rechallenge
Add a fibrate to allow the statin dose to be reduced immediately

subtopic_detail: Responding when an inpatient asks about lawfully ending their own life
stem:
You are the medical registrar on a ward in a Victorian hospital caring for a 68-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer. He has declined further chemotherapy and is receiving palliative care with reasonable symptom control.

During your morning review he asks you directly whether there is a legal way for him to end his life at a time of his choosing, and says he has been thinking about it for several weeks. He is alert and orientated, his mood is not depressed on assessment, and he has no delirium. He has decision making capacity. His pain is controlled and he is not requesting a change to his analgesia. He asks what he needs to do next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, alert and orientated, abbreviated mental test score normal, no features of delirium
data_table.Assessment: Decision making capacity intact, no depressive disorder on assessment, pain adequately controlled
data_table.Disease status: Metastatic pancreatic cancer, further chemotherapy declined, receiving palliative care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his question?

options.text: Tell him you are prohibited from discussing this subject with him
Start an antidepressant and reassess his request in four weeks
Increase his opioid dose with the intention of shortening his life
Refer him to psychiatry for a formal capacity assessment first
Answer his question and refer him for a first eligibility assessment

subtopic_detail: Abdominal pain with hyponatraemia and a raised urinary porphobilinogen
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman admitted with four days of severe generalised abdominal pain requiring repeated opioid doses. Two surgical reviews have found a soft abdomen with no guarding and no rebound, and computed tomography of her abdomen is normal.

She has vomited repeatedly and is constipated. She is anxious and mildly confused this morning and has developed weakness of both arms that is worse proximally. She started a new medication three weeks ago for acne. A nurse notes that the urine sample left on the bench has turned a dark reddish brown over several hours. Her white cell count and C reactive protein are normal and her lipase is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 162/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with no peritonism despite severe pain, proximal weakness of both arms, reduced reflexes, mild confusion, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), lipase within normal limits, computed tomography of abdomen normal, urinary porphobilinogen markedly raised
data_table.Medication: New agent started three weeks ago for acne

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous haem arginate with a high carbohydrate load
Give intravenous hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement
Give hypertonic saline to correct the sodium concentration rapidly
Give intravenous immunoglobulin for the ascending motor weakness
Give a phenobarbital loading dose to control her agitation overnight

subtopic_detail: Mucositis and pancytopenia after an inadvertent daily methotrexate dose
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who has had six days of worsening mouth ulceration so severe she cannot eat, and two days of fever.

She has taken methotrexate 15 mg once weekly for four years with stable blood counts. Her daughter brings in the dose administration aid, which a new pharmacy packed nine days ago, and you see methotrexate 15 mg packed into every single day rather than into one day each week. She takes no trimethoprim and no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug. Her renal function is mildly impaired. She has been taking folic acid 5 mg on a different day of the week as usual.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Extensive confluent oral ulceration, dry mucous membranes, no rash, no focal chest signs, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 0.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with neutrophils 0.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-155), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90) rising from a baseline of 82, alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (less than 35)
data_table.Medication error: Methotrexate 15 mg packed daily rather than weekly for the past nine days

lead_in: What is the most important specific treatment?

options.text: Give colony stimulating factor and antibiotics
Give folinic acid by intravenous injection now
Give high dose intravenous folic acid instead
Give a sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise
Give platelet and red cell transfusion support

subtopic_detail: Progressive disinhibition and apathy with preserved memory at sixty
stem:
A 60-year-old accountant is brought to your clinic by his wife, who has had to take over the household finances. Over two years he has made a series of uncharacteristic remarks to strangers, began eating large quantities of sweet food, and now sits for hours without initiating anything.

His wife says he still remembers appointments, finds his way around without difficulty and can recount last week's events accurately. He shows no concern about any of the changes. Formal cognitive testing shows preserved orientation and delayed recall, with marked impairment of planning, set shifting and response inhibition. There is no tremor, no rigidity, no gait disturbance and no visual hallucination. Magnetic resonance imaging shows asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with no vascular lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Disinhibited in interview, no insight, no parkinsonian signs, normal gait, primitive reflexes present, no focal deficit
data_table.Cognitive testing: Orientation and delayed recall preserved, marked impairment of planning, set shifting and response inhibition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function, B12 and syphilis serology all within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging shows asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy without vascular lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start donepezil and refer him to a memory service for follow up
Start risperidone to control the disinhibited behaviour long term
Refer to a cognitive service and avoid a cholinesterase inhibitor
Refer to psychiatry for treatment of a presumed depressive disorder
Reassure the couple and repeat his cognitive testing in twelve months

subtopic_detail: Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle arthritis
stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your clinic with two weeks of painful red lumps on both shins, aching swollen ankles and a low grade fever. She has a mild dry cough but is not breathless and can still run for the bus.

She was born in Australia, has never smoked, has had no tuberculosis contact and has not travelled overseas. A chest radiograph arranged by her general practitioner shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields and no parenchymal infiltrate. Her spirometry, including gas transfer, is normal. Serum calcium and creatinine are normal, her electrocardiogram is normal, and ophthalmology review today found no uveitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender erythematous nodules over both shins, bilateral ankle swelling and tenderness, chest clear on auscultation, no lymphadenopathy elsewhere, no skin plaques
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), angiotensin converting enzyme raised, interferon gamma release assay negative, spirometry with gas transfer within normal limits, electrocardiogram normal
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone and taper it over six months
Start standard four drug antituberculous therapy and notify the case
Arrange mediastinal lymph node biopsy to confirm the diagnosis first
Treat with a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug and observe her
Start methotrexate as a steroid sparing agent and review in one month

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis with absent vascularity on Doppler in a man taking amiodarone
stem:
A 67-year-old man attends your clinic with three months of weight loss of 8 kg, heat intolerance and worsening palpitations. He has taken amiodarone for two years for recurrent atrial fibrillation after other agents failed, and his rhythm had been well controlled until recently.

He has no eye signs, no goitre and no thyroid bruit. He has no family history of thyroid disease and has had no recent iodinated contrast. His thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative. Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the thyroid shows a normal sized gland with markedly reduced vascularity throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, no goitre, no thyroid bruit, no proptosis or lid lag, irregularly irregular pulse
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-25), free triiodothyronine raised, thyroid receptor antibodies negative, C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Imaging: Colour flow Doppler shows a normal sized gland with markedly reduced vascularity throughout

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start carbimazole and arrange endocrinology and cardiology review
Arrange radioactive iodine treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed
Stop the amiodarone alone and recheck his thyroid function in a month
Start potassium iodide and arrange urgent total thyroidectomy
Start prednisolone and arrange endocrinology and cardiology review
